items.a: Brittany [accept Bretagne; accept Breton; prompt on France]

items.q: It's not on an island, but Wrac'h and Ildut are prominent examples of a type of fjord found in this region known as an aber. Apothecary Cave is a sea cave on an island off the coast of this region which is known for clifftop headlands such as Raz and Pen-Hir. This region's town of Argol contains a statue of Gradlon, who ruled a city traditionally placed in this region's Bay of Douarnenez (dwar-ne-NAY), the Ker Y's, which is part of the Sea of Iroise. The basin of the Aulne separates the Aree and Noire Mountains in this region that is part of the Armorica Massif. The Gallo dialect is spoken in the eastern portion of this region. A series of canvases by Monet depicts sea stacks in this region, the Aiguilles de Port Coton. Locmariaquer (lok-ma-RI-a-ker) is a collection of stone monuments in this region's department of Morbihan. For 10 points, name this region containing the ruins of Carnac and the ports of St-Malo and Brest which is governed from its capital of Rennes on a French peninsula noted for its strong Celtic identity.
items.a: Brittany or Bretagne or Breizh or Bertaeyn or Lesser Britain

items.q: A conflict fought for control of this region is sometimes called the War of the Two Jeannes ("zhahnz"). During a war fought in this region, Robert Bemborough was slain in a large-scale duel called the Combat of the Thirty. During the Hundred Years' War, the Blois and Montfort families fought for control of this region. The myth of (*) Merlin is linked with the Paimpont forest in this region. This region shares an etymology with an island across the English Channel. This is the only region on mainland Europe to name one of the Celtic nations. Nantes and Rennes are found in, for 10 points, what peninsula and historic region of France?
items.a: Brittany [accept Breton or Bretagne; accept the War of the Breton Succession]

items.q: A "sweet and fetching little creature" from this city is told "nobody can tell if you're a woman or a man" in a song by an early lesbian singer based here. One venue in this city was called "Super-Stage" or "colorful theater." The song "[This city]'s just crazy about my legs" was often sung by a singer from here who originally performed "Falling in Love Again." A singer in this city named Jean Ross inspired the play I Am a (*) Camera and a character who sings "Maybe This Time," a signature song of Liza Minelli. In this city, Clifford Bradshaw begins a romance with singer Sally Bowles in a musical set at the Kit Kat Club, based on a Christopher Isherwood novel titled "Goodbye to [this city]." For 10 points, name this setting of Cabaret and capital of Germany.
items.a: Berlin [accept Goodbye to Berlin] (The first line is describing "Hannelore" by Claire Waldoff.)

items.q: In this city, the owner of the Violetta nightclub subsequently founded an organisation named for Chevaliere d'Eon. One song written in this city repeats that its singers are 'different from the others', the Lavender Song. One guide to this city, written by an author sometimes known as 'Aunt Magnesia', claims it is easy for people to live second lives and is named for this city's (*) 'Third Sex'. This city's clubbing scene, including clubs named Eldorado known for drag shows, were depicted by writers like Christopher Isherwood. Transvestite passes were issued in this city at the advice of its leader of the Institute for Sexology, Magnus Hirschfeld. For 10 points, name this city known for its interwar queer culture, the capital of Weimar Germany.
items.a: Berlin

items.q: In this city, the "Fast Form Manifest" style was used by Thierry Noir to create cartoonish heads that can be seen at the East Side Gallery. The film Night Crossing opens with footage of an event in this city that was also captured by Peter Leibing. Blue rope was used to fasten over 100,000 square meters of fabric in a "wrapping" of a building in this city by Christo and Jeanne-Claude. A Dmitri Vrubel mural in this city depicts a 1979 meeting in which Leonid Brezhnev shared a fraternal kiss. A watch was removed from a soldier's wrist in a photograph taken atop this city's parliament building after its capture by the Soviets. For 10 points, name this city where graffiti was broken into chunks after the 1989 fall of its namesake wall.
items.a: Berlin [accept East Berlin or Ost-Berlin; accept West Berlin; accept Berlin Wall] (The second line refers to Leibing's Leap into Freedom. The third line refers to Wrapped Reichstag. The fifth line refers to Raising a Flag over the Reichstag.)

items.q: John Beazley used this city to name an anonymous red-figure vase painter of the 5th century BC who is often contrasted with the Kleophrades Painter. The introduction of Mary Beard and John Henderson's Classical Art describes a once-armless Praying Boy sculpture called this city's "Adorant." This city often names the Severan Tondo. An artwork now located in this city contains a long staircase and a large frieze depicting the Gigantomachy. Today, this city is home to the Ishtar Gate and the Bust of Nefertiti. This city's Altes ("ALL-tiss") Museum is on its Museum Island, where an altar originally from Asia Minor is housed in the Pergamon Museum. For 10 points, name this capital that houses many works found by a native son who excavated Mycenae and Troy, Heinrich Schliemann.
items.a: Berlin [or The Berlin Painter; or Berlin Adorant; or Berlin Tondo]

items.q: The progress of Christianization in this state is linked to a stone found in the Nachtweide Marsh, the Mercury Stone, and a stone bearing a carving of pigeons surrounding a chi-rho monogram known as the Ursus Stone found beneath the old church of Pachten. The still extant Abbey of Tholey, which was first led by St. Wendel, was the first known religious community in this state. The Dollberg hosted the first fortification in what is now this state, the Otzenhausen, a rampart of the Treveri, whose ancestors also set up the menhir Gollenstein, its nation's largest. Another fortification in this state is a converted castle which is known for its informatics seminars which created the cryptographic technique DP5 named for it. That castle of (*) Dagstuhl also manages the computer science bibliography website DBLP, and this state's capital hosts the Max Planck Institute for Informatics. This state is known for a five-mile row of smelters which is part of an industrial heritage preserved by the first foundry to use blowers in gasification, the Volklingen Ironworks. This state rises from the confluence of the Prims with its namesake to the upper Weiskircher Heights in the Hunsruck Uplands, which hosts a coal basin which was transferred to France following World War I. FTP, name this western German state known for its heavy industry legacy, named for a tributary of the Moselle.
items.a: Saarland

items.q: One area of this state's second largest city promotes tourism by hiring scantily-clad meter maids to put coins in expired parking meters. Surfer's Paradise is part of a city in this state originally named for its high real estate prices and nicknamed "The Glittery Strip." This state's largest city will host the 2032 Summer Olympics. The Whitsunday Islands are part of a maritime national park in this state that stretches between its cities of (*) Mackay and Cairns. Most Torres Strait Islanders live in this state off the coast of its Cape York Peninsula. The Great Barrier Reef is off the coast of, for 10 points, which Australian state whose capital is Brisbane?
items.a: Queensland

items.q: Red sandstone cliff formations called the Cathedrals stretch along this state's Fraser Island, the world's largest sand island. The lead and silver ore mining industry in this state's interior grew out of the Mount Isa shantytown. This state's sugarcane agriculture has been damaged by an invasive species that was introduced to eliminate the native beetle population, and is centered around Bundaberg. The Kuranda Scenic Railway reaches this state's Atherton Tableland after crossing the (*) Great Dividing Range from Cairns. The Q1 skyscraper in Gold Coast, this state's surfing mecca, is the tallest building in the Southern Hemisphere. The Whitsunday Islands off this state's coast are common attractions for tourists visiting the largest structure in the world created by lifeforms. For 10 points, name this Australian state governed from Brisbane that is home to the Great Barrier Reef.
items.a: Queensland

items.q: Bernie Elsey introduced "meter maids" to this state, women in gold bikinis who used to top up almost-expired parking tickets. Boigu Island is located at this state's extreme north, off the coast of a peninsula home to the Iron Range, Lakefield and Jardine River national parks. A British explorer's confusion over the date led to a group of islands in this state being named the (*) Whitsunday Islands. Major flooding in this state in 2010 caused severe damage to its Lockyer Valley and the city of Toowoomba. This state is home to the popular tourist destination of Surfers Paradise on its Gold Coast. For 10 points, identify this "Sunshine State" of Australia, with capital at Brisbane.
items.a: Queensland

items.q: Disease-free bees are often imported from this state's Kenswick Island, part of the Whitsunday Islands once inhabited by the Ngaro people. In this state, the Surfers Paradise district brings tourists to the city of Gold Coast. Tin Can bay lies south of this state's Great Sandy Strait, which separates the mainland from (*) Fraser Island. The Torres Strait lies north of this state's Cape York Peninsula, which is east of the Gulf of Carpentaria. The Great Barrier reef brings revenue to - for 10 points - what northwestern state of Australia with capital Brisbane?
items.a: Queensland [prompt on Australia]

items.q: The blind cave scorpion Hormurus polisorum was first discovered on this island in 2001. The four endemic bird species of this island are its hawk-owl, its thrush, its white-eye, and its imperial pigeon. The bulldog rat and Maclear's rat were endemic to this island before being driven to extinction by the introduction of the black rat by settlers. An arch-shaped variety of wildlife corridors on this island is notably ascended and descended vertically by animals that spawn between November and January. Ascension Island and this island name the only two toponymically-named species of frigatebirds. A golden bosun bird appears on the green half of this island's flag. Super colonies of yellow crazy ants are currently decimating this island's namesake species of (*) red crab known for their mass migration across it, as depicted in numerous nature documentaries. The main settlement on this island is Flying Fish Cove. For 10 points, name this Indian Ocean territory of Australia named for its discovery on a December holiday.
items.a: Christmas Island

items.q: During a conflict in this province, the SS Colvile [COL-vill] transported participants from such places as Berens River. Edith Hancock was an organiser of a 1919 strike in this province which was eventually dispersed by the NWP. In 1942, officials in this province tested the readiness of residents of its largest city by launching a simulated German invasion on "What If" day. A crisis over parochial (*) language education in this province was resolved by Wilfried Laurier, known as its namesake "Schools Question." Garnet Wolseley led an 1870 expedition to this province to catch a Metis leader who launched the Red River Rebellion in 1869; that leader was Louis Riel. This province borders Saskatchewan to the west. For 10 points, name this first of the Canadian Prairie Provinces to be admitted, with its capital at Winnipeg.
items.a: Manitoba

items.q: In 1939, a proposal to lower the speed limit of this province to 50 mph for safety reasons was made by Toby Sexsmith, who also claimed that only the premier had the need to travel faster. The surveying of geologist Robert Bell allowed for the construction of the railroads that connected this province's capital to cities in the east and to its primary port. Due to an inability to acquire nails, rawhide cords called shaganappi were used in a colony in this province to fashion its namesake carts, used for transporting fur and bison products. (*) The Dawson Road was the first means of accessing this province by land and entirely within Canada and was used by the Wolseley Expedition to put down a rebellion in this province. Difficulty in communication and transportation with eastern Canada contributed to, for 10 points, which province's Red River Rebellion?
items.a: Manitoba

items.q: Winkler and Blumenort are cities found in the Pembina Valley in this province. This province's capital has a name meaning "muddy waters" in Western Cree, and it is located at the confluence of the Assiniboine and the Red rivers. This province is home to the only deep-water Arctic port in its country. That port, Churchill, is nicknamed "The Polar Bear capital of the world". This is the only prairie province with a salt-water coastline, adjoining Hudson Bay in the Northeast. For 10 points, name this Canadian province between Ontario and Saskatchewan which has its capital at Winnipeg.
items.a: Manitoba

items.q: This province contains the eastern half of a greenstone-mining belt jointly named for Snow Lake and a city named after the fictional Josiah Flintabbatey Flonatin. The largest population of Icelanders outside of Iceland is around the municipality of Gimli in this province whose capital contains the Exchange District and The Forks. British conservationist Grey Owl was an animal caretaker at this province's Riding Mountain National Park and its city of (*) Churchill is nicknamed the "Polar Bear Capital of the World." Much of this province is in the bed of the prehistoric Lake Agassiz and it is the only prairie province with coastline, since its northeast borders Hudson Bay. For 10 points, name this Canadian province between Ontario and Saskatchewan whose largest lake shares a name with its capital, Winnipeg.
items.a: Manitoba [or Le Manitoba]

items.q: The Nettilling and Amadjuak lakes are found in this region's largest island which contains such peaks as Mount Thor in its Auyuittuq National park. Cornwallis Island is separated by the Parry Channel from Devon Island to the south in this region. A culture from Kinngait near Foxe Peninsula in this region was discovered by Diamond Jenness. The Sadlermiut group that settled around Coats Island were the last remnants of the (*) Dorset culture from this region. The northernmost permanently inhabited place in the world is in this region off of Cape Sheridan and takes its name from the HMS Alert. The British Empire Range contains Barbeau Peak, the highest mountain on Ellesmere Island in this region. Frobisher Bay can be found on Baffin Island in this region. For 10 points, name this primarily Inuit northern Canadian territory whose capital is Iqaluit.
items.a: Nunavut [accept Baffin Island on the leadin]

items.q: A performing arts troupe from this region called "Artcirq" was founded by Isuma Productions to reduce its suicide rates. Most scholars believe this territory contains an island referred to as "Helluland." A culture named for a geographic feature in this region was the first discovered by Diamond Jenness. One island in this territory contains Lake Hazen, whose only species of fish is char. The aforementioned culture from this territory is named for Cape Dorset and was displaced by the Thule people. This territory contains the Challenger Mountains, and its highest point is Barbeau peak. The Eureka research base in this region reports a permanent population of zero, while its Alert base is the northernmost permanently-inhabited location in the world. The capital of this region used to be named Frobisher Bay. For 10 points, name this territory that includes Ellesmere Island and has its capital at Iqaluit, the northernmost and newest territory of Canada.
items.a: Nunavut

items.q: Photosynthetic organisms called hypoliths are found in large quantities on this territory's Devon and Cornwallis Islands. The medieval Dorset culture flourished in this modern day territory, whose northernmost point lies south of the Lincoln Sea. The Belcher Islands are a part of this territory, whose highest point is Barbeau Peak. The northernmost permanently inhabited place in the world, (*) Alert, is located on an island in this territory. The cities of Whale Cove and Rankin Inlet are located in this territory, which includes most of the western shore of the Hudson Bay. This territory, which includes Ellesmere Island, has a capital that lies between two peninsulas on Frobisher Bay. For 10 points, name this most recently incorporated and primarily Inuit Canadian territory, whose capital is Iqaluit.
items.a: Nunavut

items.q: The community of Rankin Inlet in this territory lost a plebiscite to be the capital when this territory was first established. In July 2015, this territory's community of Repulse Bay changed its name to Naujaat. This territory's highest point is Barbeau Peak, located in the British Empire Range on this territory's Ellesmere Island. This territory is home to the military base CFB Alert, which is the northernmost permanently inhabited settlement in the world. This territory split from the Northwest Territories in 1999. For 10 points, name this Canadian arctic territory whose capital is Iqaluit, populated mostly by Inuit.
items.a: Nunavut

items.q: A premier of this province, former lacrosse goalie Boss Johnson, lost power in 1952, setting up 20 years of rule of W. A. C. Bennett of the Social Credit Party. The "father" of this province, James Douglas, championed the Cariboo Road to settle its interior. An infrastructure project agreed to as part of this province joining a confederation led to a scandal that brought down the government of (*) John A. Macdonald. During World War II, this province's Okanagan Valley received forcibly relocated people of Japanese heritage. The Pig War emerged from an 1846 treaty setting this modern-day province's southern border despite efforts from the "Fifty-four Forty or Fight!" faction. For 10 points, name this Canadian province home to Vancouver.
items.a: British Columbia [or BC]

items.q: This province is allegedly home to the Ogopogo lake monster. The main TED Talk conference has been hosted in this province's largest city since 2014. The 2010 Winter Olympics were hosted in cities in this province, including its resort town Whistler. The Hecate Strait separates the Haida Gwaii from this province's mainland. This province's capital (*) Victoria is home to a museum whose First Nations artifacts include totem poles. The Strait of Juan de Fuca runs across part of this province's southern border with the state of Washington. For 10 points, name this westernmost Canadian province, home to Vancouver Island.
items.a: British Columbia

items.q: Prior to beginning a journey to the national capital elsewhere, workers in this province were organized by Arthur "Slim" Evans for the "On to Ottawa" Trek. The 1858 Fraser Canyon Gold Rush occurred in this province. The Tsimshian (SEEM-she-ann) and Kwakiutl (KWA-kil-to) mainly live in this province on an (*) island named for a British naval captain. A city in this province was the western terminus of the Canadian Pacific transcontinental railway and hosted the 2010 Winter Olympics. For 10 points, name this province whose most populous city is Vancouver.
items.a: British Columbia

items.q: In this province, a giant pile of bright yellow sulfur is visible from Lions Gate Bridge. This province's many fjord lakes include Okanagan Lake, which borders its city of Kelowna. A city in this province is home to the neighborhoods of Cold Harbor and Gastown and is separated from Richmond and Surrey by the Fraser River. An island home to (*) Nanaimo and this province's capital is bordered on the south by the Strait of Juan de Fuca. This province contains the Whistler Blackcomb Ski Resort, which was a venue for the 2010 Winter Olympics. Victoria is the capital of, for 10 points, what Western Canadian province whose largest city is Vancouver?
items.a: British Columbia [or BC]

items.q: A non-Sicilian Constanza di Hohenstaufen's marriage to the heir of this kingdom increased its royalty's opulence, as shown by their lavish soap purchases. A monk who ruled this kingdom for three years left his wife and abdicated after his older brother, nicknamed "The Battler," died childless. This kingdom's monarchy held the Dukedom of Athens for most of the 14th century. A ruler of this kingdom penned a (*) "Book of Deeds" that included his conquest of the Balearic Islands. This kingdom's ruling house was the ultimate beneficiary of the War of the Sicilian Vespers, but its inability to pay its soldiers led to the creation of the mercenary Catalan Company. This is the smaller of the two kingdoms united by the marriage of the Catholic Monarchs. For 10 points, name this kingdom whose ruler Ferdinand married Isabella of Castile.
items.a: Aragon [or Kingdom of Aragon or Reino de Aragon Regne d'Arago or Reino d'Aragon]

items.q: This kingdom sent an emissary to the court of Abaqa Khan in an ill-fated attempt to organize what would become known as the 1269 Crusade of the Infants. A group of soldiers from this kingdom defeated the Karasid beylik at the 1303 Battle of Cyzicus and seized the lands of Walter V around Athens after the Battle of Halmyros. A ruler of this kingdom was killed after his army's defeat at the Battle of Muret, the last major battle of the Albigensian Crusade. This kingdom changed dynasties when its queen Petronilla married Count Ramon Berenguer IV. After anti-French riots, Peter III of this kingdom defeated Charles I of Anjou in the War of the Sicilian Vespers. This kingdom's ruler James I conquered Valencia from the Almohads. For 10 points, name this Spanish kingdom that was ruled by Ferdinand II when he married Isabella of Castille.
items.a: Aragon [or Kingdom of Aragon or Crown of Aragon; or Reino d'Aragon; or Regne d'Arago; or Regnum Aragonum; or Reino de Aragon]

items.q: After this kingdom won a war, it and the losing side both began calling their own territory "this side of the lighthouse" and the other's "beyond the lighthouse." After the death of a ruler of this kingdom, its succession laws were addressed in the Compromise of Caspe ("KASS-pay"). That ruler of this kingdom conquered the Judicate of Arborea. The "evil customs" in this kingdom were ended after a 15th-century rebellion of the remences ("ruh-MEN-suhs"). A mercenary band named for a possession of this kingdom was formed by Roger de Flor ("roo-ZHAY duh FLO") after the ruler of this kingdom was invited to depose Charles I of Anjou by the Sicilian Vespers. The Kingdom of Majorca was created by this kingdom's ruler James the Conqueror. For 10 points, name this kingdom whose later monarch, Ferdinand II, married Isabelle of Castile.
items.a: Aragon [or Kingdom of Aragon, Crown of Aragon, Reino d'Aragon, or Regne d'Arago; prompt on Principality of Catalonia, Principat de Catalunya, Principado de Cataluna, Kingdom of Valencia, Regne de Valencia, Reino de Valencia, County of Barcelona, Comtat de Barcelona, or House of Barcelona by asking "what larger kingdom was it part of?"]

items.q: One ruler of this kingdom sent an embassy to Abaqa Khan of the Ilkhanate and compiled the 'Book of the Consulate of the Sea' as well as the autobiographical 'Book of Deeds'. That king of this kingdom also signed the Treaty of Capdepera after defeating Abu Yahya in one campaign. After a ruler of this kingdom known as 'the Great' pressed the claim of his wife Constance II to one throne, Martin IV declared a crusade against this kingdom as part of the War of the Sicilian Vespers. During that war, this kingdom fought against its former territory of Majorca. A later princess of this kingdom was first married to Arthur, Prince of Wales. For 10 points, name this kingdom whose ruler Ferdinand II married Isabella of Castile.
items.a: Aragon

items.q: A town in this island's north became a ghost town after villagers were killed in a 1915 bear attack. A glass pyramid whose name translates to "sunny spot" can be found in a park designed in this island's largest city. Sagas called yukar were passed down by this island's native people, who traditionally tattooed the mouths of their women as a transition to adulthood. Green algae balls can be found in a caldera lake in this island's Akan National Park. This island's largest city hosts over 300 ice sculptures during its annual snow festival. The northern terminus of the Seikan Tunnel is the city of Hakodate on this island, the traditional home of the Ainu people. Sapporo is the largest city on, for 10 points, what northernmost of Japan's four major islands?
items.a: Hokkaido

items.q: This island's lack of monkeys placed it just north of Blakiston's ("BLACK"-is-tunz) Line. The native people of this island now practice a modified version of the Iomante (eye-oh-MAN-tay) ritual, in which a bear cub is raised alongside humans, but no longer sacrificed. The Nemuro (NEH-mu-roh) strait separates this island from Kunashir (KUN-uh-sheer) Island, and the La Perouse strait separates it from Sakhalin (SAA-kuh-lin). This island is the northern terminus of the world's longest (*) underwater tunnel, which crosses the Tsugaru (SOO-gaa-roo) strait. The 1972 Olympics were held at this island's capital, Sapporo (SAA-poh-roh). The Seikan (SAY-ken) tunnel connects this island to Honshu to the south. For 10 points, name this home of the Ainu people, the northernmost of Japan's four main islands.
items.a: Hokkaido [prompt on Ezo; generously prompt on Japan or Nippon or Nihon or Nippon-koku or Nihon-koku]

items.q: While teaching at an agricultural college on this island, William S. Clark introduced the raising of livestock and imported crops from America. This is the southernmost island in the otter trade described by Jerome de Angelis run by a people who pushed into a region north of this island, displacing the Nivkh. A rebel government on this island used four brigades led by French officers and an army trained by Jules Brunet to defend a star fort. The last phase of the (*) Boshin War saw its eventual losers retreat to this island and found the Republic of Ezo. The Matsumae clan dominated this island, which was unified as a single prefecture due to settlement by ethnic Japanese people during the Meiji Restoration. For 10 points, name this island, historically home to the Ainu people, the northernmost in Japan.
items.a: Hokkaido [accept Ezo before it is read]

items.q: The phrase "Boys, be ambitious" was popularized on this island by William S. Clark, an American professor who established an agricultural college here. The last public performance of soprano Maria Callas ("CAL-uss") was held in 1974 in this island's largest city. A breakaway republic on this island was established by French army officer Jules Barnet. Shakushain's revolt was led on this island in the late 1660s against its governing Matsumae clan. The Republic of Ezo on this island, the first democracy in its country, was established in the aftermath of the Boshin War by Tokugawa officials fleeing from the Meiji Restoration. This island's native people practice bear sacrifice in the Iyomante ritual. The Ainu people are native to, for 10 points, what northernmost Japanese island?
items.a: Hokkaido

items.q: A 25-year public health study in the north of this region used a community intervention model to cut heart disease rates from what had been the highest in the world in 1972. A large type of spitz bred to harry bears in this region is appropriately named the Bear Dog. The 22-dome Church of the Transfiguration is the centerpiece of an all-wood religious complex built on an island in this region in the 18th century. Koli National Park became a tourist destination during a late (*) 19th-century romantic revival that promoted the folk culture of this region, which provided subjects for painters like Louis Sparre and Akseli Gallen-Kallela. During his fifteen years of collecting runic songs on field trips mostly taken in this region, Elias Lonnrot published Kanteletar and the Kalevala. For 10 points, Lake Ladoga is on the southern border of what historical region split between Finland and Russia?
items.a: Karelia [accept Republic of Karelia; accept West Karelia, North Karelia, South Karelia, East Karelia, Russian Karelia, Border Karelia, or Finnish Karelia; accept Karelianism; accept Karelian Bear Dog; accept the North Karelia Project; prompt on Finland or Eastern Finland; prompt on Russia or North-Western Russia] (The religious complex is Kizhi Pogost.)

items.q: This European region's native dishes include kalitka pastries and salted, marinated mushrooms, the latter of which were popularized when nearly half a million refugees from this region were resettled after a treaty signed by Rudolf Walden. Removing foreigners from this region was the goal of the Sword Scabbard Declaration. Reconquering this region was the goal of the Viena and Aunus expeditions, part of the broader Kinship Wars. Historically, industry in this region relied on a canal which terminated at (*) Vyborg and is named for Lake Saimaa. This region comprised the [emphasize] northernmost territories ceded by the Treaty of Nystad. Gustav Mannerheim repeatedly sought to annex the eastern portion of this region, most of which was transferred to the Soviet Union via the 1940 Moscow Peace Treaty that concluded the Winter War. For 10 points, name this region which borders Lake Ladoga and the White Sea and is divided between Russia and Finland.
items.a: Karelia [accept East Karelia; prompt on Finland]

items.q: A Saudi-born leader of a militia based in this polity was assassinated with a poisonous letter addressed from his mother. Following a botched rescue operation, gunmen in this polity beheaded four kidnapped Granger Telecom engineers. Rebels based in this polity were controversially targeted in a neighboring region in 2004 by Shmel rockets. On Knowledge Day, terrorists from this polity occupied a school in neighboring (*) Beslan. In response to a coup by Dzhokhar ("jo-KHAHR") Dudayev, this polity was weakly invaded by Boris Yeltsin. A series of 1999 apartment bombings and the invasion of nearby Dagestan provoked a crackdown on this republic that brought Vladimir Putin to power. For 10 points, name this Ramzan Kadyrov-led, majority-Muslim Russian republic in the Caucasus.
items.a: Chechnya [or Chechen Republic; or Chechen Republic of Ichkeria] (The first clue refers to Ibn al-Khattab.)

items.q: Peter Kennedy and Darren Hickey were among four telecom workers who were kidnapped and killed in this region. Residents of this region were deported to Central Asia as part of Operation Lentil. The terrorist group Riyad as-Saliheen (ree-YAD us-SAH-lih-heen) was formed in this region and carried out the 2004 Beslan school massacre. A president of this region was killed in a 2004 stadium bomb blast; that man, Akhmat Kadyrov (OK-mot KAH-dih-rov), has since been succeeded by his son Ramzan. A war in this region spread into neighboring Ingushetia (in-goo-SHET-ee-ah) and ended with the Khasav-Yurt accord. For 10 points, name this region of the Caucasus where the Islamic republic of Ichkeria (itch-CARE-ee-ah) briefly established independence from the Russian Federation in the 1990s.
items.a: Chechnya [or Ichkeria until it is read; prompt on Caucasus]

items.q: In August 2016, this territory's capital hosted a conference at which Ahmad al-Tayeb, the Grand Imam of Al-Azhar, excluded Salafis in a definition of Sunni Islam. In July 2016, this territory's leader launched a reality TV show called The Team in which participants compete to be his assistant. This territory's capital is the site of a mosque named after its former leader Akhmad, who was also its current leader's father. Prior to 1991, this territory was combined with its western neighbor (*) Ingushetia. This territory ruled by Ramzan Kadyrov is bordered to the east by Dagestan. Ichkeria is a name for this territory that was used by a separatist government of this territory that became the Caucasus Emirate. For 10 points, Grozny is the capital of which predominantly-Muslim Russian republic?
items.a: Chechnya [or Chechen Republic; accept Ichkeria before it is read]

items.q: During a 1958 ethnic riot in this region, people on one side donned red headbands to identify themselves to authorities. The natives of this region were targeted in Operation Lentil, which included the Khaibakh massacre and the forced deportation of much of its population. The Sunzha River runs through this region, and once flowed past a presidential palace used by (*) Dzhokhar Dudayev. FSB forces killed another leader of this region, Aslan Maskhadov, and its separatist movement is now led by Akhmed Zakayev. Found near Dagestan and Ingushetia, this Muslim-dominated region declared independence as Ichkeria in 1991. For 10 points, name this southern Russian republic, the site of a bloody war in the 1990s.
items.a: Chechnya

items.q: Whether to place certain elements where wooden beams would have been placed or to rearrange them for greater symmetry forms a namesake corner problem for this order. Those elements, triglyphs, occur below the architrave and alternate with metopes, which in one famous example feature sculptures of the battle between the Lapiths and the Centaurs. Employed in the Lincoln memorial, its columns do not rest on a base. For 10 points, identify this simplest order of classical Greek architecture, most famously used in the Parthenon.
items.a: Doric order

items.q: Minor details which can help identify this style include the use of a plinth on which the supports sit and the presence of dentils above the frieze, which is typically carved in relief. Its columns are sharply fluted and measure about ten base diameters in height. According to legend, it was invented by the architect Callimachus who was inspired by a covered basket through which an acanthus plant had grown. The leaves of the acanthus are still found at the top of this kind of column, the Classical order most favored by the Romans. For 10 points, name this style of architecture that evolved from the Doric and the Ionic.
items.a: Corinthian Order

items.q: Augustus Saint-Gaudens' facade for the Albright-Knox Art Gallery in Buffalo features four of these objects representing Art, Music, Painting and Sculpture. Fritz Koenig's sculpture The Sphere, which survived the 9/11 attacks, was originally named for one of these objects. Cambodian carvings likely inspired a series of Amedeo Modigliani drawings of these objects, and Auguste Rodin depicted a collapsed one of these objects supporting an uncarved stone. The name for these objects may derive from a cult of Artemis named for a "Walnut Tree," while Vitruvius claimed they were named after (*) slave women marched out of a city conquered by Sparta. A variant of these objects depicted carrying baskets are called canephora and represent devotees of the aspect of Athena that names these objects. Six of these objects support the porch of the Erechtheion of the Acropolis in Athens. For 10 points name these columns in the shape of female figures.
items.a: caryatids [prompt on columns]

items.q: Thomas Shields Clarke created a series of these works representing seasons, and three of these are found outside the Warsaw Supreme Court building. Ones representing Architecture and Music are found in the Saint-Gaudens designed Albright-Knox Gallery in Buffalo. It's not the Discobolus or a Venus, but Charles Townley acquired one of these figures from the Villa Montalto which is currently in the British Museum. The Canopus View of Hadrian's villa contains a series of these figures. The Erechtheion has a (*) porch named for the fact that it contains six of these figures, one of which was removed as part of the Elgin marbles. These figures, whose counterparts are called telamon or atlas, often have a basket or entablature on their heads. For 10 points, name these architectural supports that take the shape of women.
items.a: caryatid [prompt on things like "statues" or "statues of women"]

items.q: A style of gown from this movement with loose box pleats was named after an artist who frequently painted them. A portrait of a patron of this movement shows her reclining in a dark blue dress while holding an open book. That patron of this movement commissioned herself as Amitie offering herself to another pendant sculpture. A painting from this movement includes a stone sculpture of a "menacing" Cupid on the left. That painting from this movement, recently restored by the Wallace Collection, depicts a man in the bushes watching his lover kick off a slipper as she uses the title object. Madame de Pompdour commissioned portraits in this movement from Francois Boucher. For 10 points, name this ornate movement exemplified by Jean-Honore Fragonard's The Swing.
items.a: Rococo [or Late Baroque; prompt on Baroque]

items.q: Flora Yukhnovich's work heavily features notable paintings from this period, changing their subjects to abstract and fluid forms. This style was introduced to Munich via the design of the Amalienburg palace. A sculptor from this period notably made many sculptures of drunken nymphs in terracottFrederick the Great names a unique variation of the art movement, (*) which influenced his Sanssouci palace and of which adherents include architect Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff. Many works of British furniture in this period were made by Thomas Chippendale. For 10 points, name this art movement of Clodion, Antoine Watteau and Jean-Honore Fragonard, whose name comes from a variation of the French word for a pearl-based method of decoration, rocaille.
items.a: rococo

items.q: One artist who worked in this style carved the terracotta reliefs Faun Family and The Intoxication of Wine. The sculptor Clodion worked in this style, as did an artist depicted in Self-portrait in a Straw Hat. This style was pioneered by an artist who included The Pursuit and The Lover Crowned in his (*) Progress of Love series; in another painting by that artist, a man hides in some bushes and a woman throws her shoe into the air while riding the title implement. Jean-Honore Fragonard's The Swing is part of, for 10 points, what ornate eighteenth-century French art movement?
items.a: Rococo [or Late Baroque; prompt on Baroque alone]

items.q: This art movement influenced the cabinets made by Thomas Chippendale, and one artist from it created two paintings depicting Jupiter seducing Callisto while he was disguised as Diana. That artist also made several portraits of Madame de Pompadour, who helped popularize this art movement. Francois (*) Boucher [boo-shay] was an artist from this movement, and another of its members depicted a fete galante in The Embarkation for Cythera. A later painting in this style shows a woman kicking off her shoe while on a swing. For 10 points, name this post-Baroque art movement whose members include Jean-Antoine Watteau and Jean-Honore Fragonard.
items.a: Rococo

items.q: A lithographed poster in this style advertises Sarah Bernhardt's performance in Victorien Sardou's play Gismonda. A house in this style which has mosaics featuring whiplash curving lines and a wrought-iron balcony is the Hotel Tassel. That is one of four townhouses in Brussels designed in this style by Victor Horta. This style is exemplified by the flowery (*) advertisements of Alphonse Mucha. Favrile glass was used to make lamps in this style by Louis Comfort Tiffany. Hector Guimard's ("ghee-MAR") entrances to the Paris Metro are in, for 10 points, what decorative style with a French name?
items.a: Art Nouveau

items.q: This style was adopted by a "school" of artisans in Nancy, including furniture designer Louis Majorelle and the Daum crystal studio. This movement, which took its name from the gallery of Siegfried Bing, was revived in the 1960s for the design of "psychedelic" posters. This style was used to decorate the interior of Brussel's Hotel (*) Tassel, and it was promoted by the magazine Jugend [YOO-gunt], which gave rise to the Munich and Vienna "Secessions." "Dragonfly" and "lily-of-the-valley" designs were used in a set of works in this style by Hector Guimard [gee-MAR]. The Arts and Crafts Movement inspired many lamps in this style designed by the "Tiffany Girls." Curving, plant-based forms characterize-for 10 points-what style whose French name means "new art?"
items.a: Art Nouveau [prompt on Jugendstil]

items.q: This term can be used for work as diverse as that of Otto Wagner and Joseph Olbrich, who opposed Wagner's classicism and formed the Vienna Secession. It is exemplified by Victor Horta's Hotel Tassel, inspired by the works of Charles Rennie Macintosh. Architect Hector Guimard used it for the Paris Metro signs, and it also popped up as Spain's "modernisme" and Germany's Jugendstil (YOO gind shteel). For 10 points, name this movement also practiced by Antonio Gaudi and shown at the Universal Exposition of 1900, exemplified by the painting of Gustav Klimt and the glassmaking of Louis Tiffany.
items.a: Art Nouveau [accept Jugendstil before it is read; prompt on modernisme before it is read]

items.q: This movement was promoted through the magazine Ver Sacrum, and was advocated in Belgium by Les Vingt, including Ensor and Horta, but it did not survive World War I. Known as Stile Liberty in Italy and as Floreale in Spain, this movement took its name from an interior design gallery in Paris. A reaction against the historical art of the mid-19th century, this richly ornamented and asymmetrical style often included plant tendrils and other erotic nature. Seen in the architecture of Rennie Mackintosh, the glassware of Lalique, and the works of Klimt, For 10 points, identify this art movement embraced by designers like Tiffany whose name literally translates as "new art."
items.a: Art Nouveau

items.q: Le Courbusier is said to have coined the name of this artistic movement in a series of articles about a 1925 Paris exhibition. A district in Miami is named after this eclectic artistic movement. This movement replaced the organic shapes of Art Nouveau with geometric lines. This artistic movement, also sometimes called (*) style moderne, emphasized a "streamlined" look. Primarily known for architecture, this interwar movement incorporated many man-made materials, such as Bakelite. For 10 points, name this artistic style of the 1920's and 30's, examples of which include the Chrysler Building.
items.a: Art Deco [or style moderne until it is read]

items.q: This style was prefigured by the neo-Byzantine Nebraska State Capitol, which was imitated by the State Capitol of Louisiana and the Los Angeles Public Library. Near the end of his career, Henri Sauvage designed the department store La Samaritaine in this style. The tallest brick building in the world is in this style, and is topped by seven terraced "arches" of stainless steel with a triangular (*) sunburst pattern; that was designed by William Van Alen. This style has "Zigzag" and "Streamlined" Moderne substyles. A building in this style includes a spire originally intended for dirigibles, and was designed by Shreve, Lamb & Harmon. Another building in this style was the tallest in the world for 11 months, before being topped by another Manhattan skyscraper in this style. For 10 points, name this hit style of the 1920s and 1930s, exemplified by the Chrysler Building and Empire State Building.
items.a: Art Deco [prompt on "Style Moderne"]

items.q: Wiener Werkstatte was the primary source of this and the first building in this style, which is in Helskinki, features four giant figures holding a globe of light each. The Barclay-Vesey Building was the first skyscraper to be created in this style and it was eventually overtaken by the Streamline Moderne style. John and Donald B. Parkinson and William Van Alen were architects who designed in this style, whose name came from a 1925 Exposition in Paris. For 10 points, name this architectural style of the 1920s and 1930s that often featured a zigzag motif and is most famous for being the style in which the Chrysler Building was designed.
items.a: Art Deco

items.q: A "New" version of this architectural style was coined by Alison Smithson to describe the design of Smithdon High School in Hunstanton. A building in this style in Preston features four upward-curving balconies running parallel across its facade. A now-demolished library in this style was designed by John Madin in an "inverted (*) ziggurat" design and was described by the then-Prince Charles as resembling a "place where books are incinerated, not kept". The London Symphony Orchestra is based at a performing arts centre designed in this style that is part of the City of London's Barbican estate. For 10 points, name this modern architectural style characterised by angular shapes and exposed brick and concrete.
items.a: Brutalism [accept brutalist architecture or New Brutalism; prompt on modernism or modernist architecture] <JDC, Other Fine Arts>

items.q: A theorist who supports this movement used the example of Antoni Gaudi's ‎Casa Batllo ("bull-YOH") as being "multivalent," one of his requirements for the creation of "cosmogenic architecture." A building from this movement features a giant copper statue by Raymond Kaskey atop a pedestal extending out from the green podium that makes up its first two stories. "Radical eclecticism" advocate Charles Jencks describes this movement's predecessor as dying when the "final coup de grace by dynamite" destroyed the Pruitt-Igoe Housing Project. A cube-shaped building from this movement has white stucco facades interrupted by a grid of square shaped windows and (*) dark trapezoidal wedges. Both Michael Graves's Portland Building and a building with an open pediment called a "Chippendale" are part of this movement. For 10 points, Philip Johnson's AT&T Building is part of what post-1960's movement that deliberately juxtaposed Classical and contemporary architectural elements as a reaction to the rigidity and lack of ornamentation of the International Style?
items.a: postmodernism [or postmodern architecture]

items.q: Kenneth Frampton highlighted early Czech influence on this movement, such as the functionalist Bata Shoe Store. A building from this movement is made of gunite ("gun"-ite) sprayed onto a steel frame and has two Ford Model-A headlights in its staircase. The Lovell House by Richard Neutra was included in a Henry-Russell Hitchcock MoMA exhibition coining this movement's name, which he curated with (*) Philip Johnson. In a building from this movement, decorative bronze I-beams frame the grid of windows that makes up its curtain wall. The "corporate architecture" of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill was influenced by an architect who justified this style with the dictum "less is more." For 10 points, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe's Seagram Building is a "glass box" from what mid-20th century movement?
items.a: International Style [prompt on modernism or modern architecture; or internationalism; accept functionalism before mention; accept rationalism; accept Neue Sachlichkeit or New Objectivity; do not accept or prompt on "Bauhaus"]

items.q: Students of an artist from this movement who called themselves the "Marli Weavers" included Claire Zeisler and Lenore Tawney. In 2009, Krueck and Sexton restored a curtain made by that artist from this movement, who was the dedicatee of a coffee and tea set that included a flat-topped teapot made of ebony and nickel silver. An artist from this movement used bent plywood to create many chaises longues and made his "Model B3" chair from steel. Ancient (*) Peruvian textiles inspired an artist from this movement who worked alongside Marianne Brandt and Marcel Breuer. Josef and Anni Albers came to Black Mountain College while members of this movement. The future Chicago School of Design was founded by an artist from this movement, Laszlo Moholy-Nagy. For 10 points, name this Weimar-era school of design led by Walter Gropius.
items.a: Bauhaus [or Staatliches Bauhaus; accept New Bauhaus; prompt on modernism] (The first clue refers to Marli Ehrmann.)

items.q: Three members of this institution once stayed at the Isokon flats in London, one of whom created its namesake "Long chair". One member of this institution created "Telephone pictures," which were constructed by an enamel factory. That artist filmed (*) A Lightplay, which he created in his Light Space Modulator. The wife of one of the founding members of this school had had an affair with Oskar Kokoschka, and had previously been married to Gustav Mahler. Herbert Bayer designed this school's namesake sans-serif font. A member of this school created the Wassily chair, named for another lecturer at the school. For 10 points, identify this school, formerly headed by Walter Gropius and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, whose faculty included Laszlo Moholy-Nagy and Marcel Breuer.
items.a: the Bauhaus

items.q: One teacher here, Johannes Itten, promoted the Mazdaznan cult. The foundation course at this school was taught by Laszlo Moholy-Nagy (pr. NAHZH), and a museum dedicated to this school can be found in the White City of Tel Aviv. Its second head, Hannes Meyer, was dismissed from the city of Dessau in 1930 due to "Communist machinations." It was permanently closed rather than accede to Nazi demands to replace Vassily Kandinsky by its final director, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. For the point, what Weimar-era Modernist German art school was founded by Walter Gropius?
items.a: Bauhaus

items.q: An artist who worked in this style included two maids huddling around Elizabeth and Mary in his version of The Visitation. The first woman artist documented to have painted female nudes, Lavinia Fontana, primarily painted in this style. Sweden's Skokloster Castle houses a portrait painted in a "Northern" form of this style that depicts Rudolf II as an assemblage of vegetables. Cupid cradles Venus's (*) breasts in a work in this style; that work also depicts pink petals being clutched by Folly. Mary, who poses figura serpentinata, cradles an oversized baby Jesus in a painting in this style titled Madonna with a Long Neck. For 10 points, what late Renaissance art style exemplified by the exaggeration of bodily features was practiced by Parmagianino?
items.a: Mannerism [or Mannerist; accept Northern Mannerism; accept late Renaissance until "late Renaissance" is read; prompt on maniera; reject "Renaissance"] (The painting in the first line was created by Jacopo da Pontormo.)

items.q: An artist from this movement had assistants burn furniture to maintain the heat to successfully cast a bronze sculpture in the Piazza della Signoria. Giambologna's Abduction of a Sabine Woman, a sculpture from this movement, depicts three figures in the movement's common figura serpentinata style. Perseus with the Head of Medusa was sculpted by Benevenuto Cellini, a sculptor from this movement. A self-portrait at 21 with an unusually large (*) right hand was painted by an artist from this movement who also painted a large baby Jesus held by the title Madonna with the Long Neck. For 10 points, name this Late Renaissance movement of Parmigianino that depicted elongated features and exaggerated forms.
items.a: Mannerism [or Mannerist; accept Northern Mannerism]

items.q: A crucial to the formation of this movement included works such as Diana the Huntress and was the School of Fontainebleau. The leader of that school painted a ladder-filled Deposition scene while another artist in this movement painted a more pastel-shaded Deposition. This style of Rosso Fiorentino is used in a painting featuring Time sweeping his arm out to the right while (*) Folly prepares to throw rose petals on the goddess of love embracing her son. The most notable work from this movement shows a tiny St. Jerome holding a scroll while a large, long infant Jesus sits in the lap of Mary, The Madonna with the Long Neck. For 10 points, name this late-Renaissance school of art that focused on elongated proportions and figures.
items.a: Mannerism [accept word forms such as Mannerist art; accept late Renaissance until mentioned; anti-prompt on School of Fontainebleau until mentioned]

items.q: One painting from this art movement features unusually bright colors and notably lacks a cross. Another painting from this movement depicts a putto [poo-toe] preparing to throw roses onto a mother and son posed in figura serpentinata [ser-pen-ti-nah-ta]. Those works from this movement are a Deposition by Pontormo and (*) Bronzino's Venus, Cupid, Folly, and Time. This movement's use of unnatural colors and perspective can also be seen in the works of El Greco. For 10 points, name this Late Renaissance art movement known for its elongated figures.
items.a: mannerism

items.q: An advocate of this style wrote that buildings should have no unnecessary features and that ornament should only enrich a building's construction in the two "great rules" of design he put forth in the book Contrasts. The term "streaky bacon style" was used to deride red brick buildings of this movement, which was advocated by the Camden Society and its journal, The Ecclesiologist (eh-KLEEZ-ee-"ologist"). The best-known room of an early building in this style is a picture gallery with crimson walls and a papier-mache fan vault ceiling. A memorial in this style consists of a ornate pavilion over a gold statue of a prince and was designed by the architect of the St. Pancras Hotel, George Gilbert Scott. This movement is exemplified by Augustus Pugin's work on the Houses of Parliament and by Eugene Viollet-le-Duc's (ooh-ZHEN vee-oh-LAY-le-dook's) fanciful restorations. This movement is so named because it was inspired by the style Abbot Suger (soo-zhay) used for the Basilica of St. Denis (sahn-dah-NEE). For 10 points, name this architectural movement, which adapted elements such as flying buttresses from a namesake medieval architecture style.
items.a: Gothic Revival [or neo-Gothic; or Victorian Gothic; prompt on Gothic, Christian, or Pointed architecture]

items.q: Just before the coda, a piano piece in this genre suddenly drops from the tonic of D-flat major to the A major of its "B" section. A C-sharp-minor piece in this genre begins with both hands playing quarter-note quadruplets in 3-4 time. Chopin's first piece in this genre begins with a high, fortissimo C-sharp half-diminished chord with a B on top and a G on the bottom, which is held for 4 bars before cadencing in the tonic of B minor. Despite being his Opus 4, Johannes Brahms's earliest extant piece is an E-flat-minor work in this genre that rips off Chopin's second piece in this genre, which is in (*) B-flat minor. Chopin used 3-4 time and the tempo marking "Presto" for all of his works in this genre, and he only used a major key for his last one, in E major. Chopin's ballades are often paired with his four highly virtuosic works in this genre. The second movements of Chopin's last two sonatas have this title, as opposed to his first sonata, which has a minuet. For 10 points, name this genre whose name is Italian for "joke."
items.a: scherzos [or scherzi]

items.q: Johannes Brahms's earliest surviving work, his Opus 4, is a piano piece of this title in E-flat minor; Brahms also composed the section of this name from the F-A-E Sonata. The so-called "Russian" quartets from Joseph Haydn's Opus 33 are sometimes named after this word because, oddly for their time, each of them contains a movement with this name. Ludwig van Beethoven may have used an Austrian pilgrims' hymn as the basis for a movement of this name. A very short movement with this name flips the the theme from the opening Allegro into B-flat major in Beethoven's (*) "Hammerklavier" sonata. Beethoven's 7th symphony contains a movement of this name played at presto speed. One of Beethoven's major innovations in symphonic form was to replace traditional third movement minuet and trio with movements of this name. For 10 points, give this name for a light-hearted musical movement, whose name literally means "joke" in Italian.
items.a: scherzo

items.q: The second of Felix Mendelssohn's three Opus 16 fantasies for piano is one of these pieces. Chopin wrote four unusually dark examples of these pieces, including his Opus 20 and his Opus 31. Mendelssohn's incidental music to A Midsummer Night's Dream includes one of these pieces after the overture. The third movement of nearly all of Bruckner's symphonies is one of these pieces, since it was the main form of the third movement of the Romantic symphony. Beethoven's symphonies replaced the minuet with one of these pieces, which is usually played quickly and humorously. For 10 points, identify this type of piece, whose name is Italian for "joke."
items.a: scherzo [or scherzi]

items.q: An artwork in this medium features a model of a church organ sitting next to a statue of Jupiter Tonans and is named after Kynzvart Castle. A person getting their shoe shined can be seen at the bottom-left of a work in this medium that depicts the Boulevard du Temple. After secretly showing works in this medium to Francois Arago, their creator got into a (*) patent battle with Henry Fox Talbot, who had developed a rival process that used "salted paper." This medium's creator previously worked with Nicephore Niepce on the Heliograph. Works in this medium were created by blowing mercury vapor onto a silver-coated copper plate and then dipping it into a salt bath. For 10 points, give this medium, named after a French pioneer of photography.
items.a: daguerreotypes [prompt on photographs or photography]

items.q: A proper approach to this technique is central to Leon Battista Alberti's treatise On Painting. Ceiling painters like Melozzo da Forli used a form of this technique known as sotto in su to create trompe-l'œil ("tromp loy") frescoes. Filippo Brunelleschi is credited with discovering this technique, which he popularized by having viewers look at a (*) mirror through holes in his paintings. When using this technique, all orthogonals converge at a point along the horizon line, known as the vanishing point. For 10 points, name this artistic technique that scales the size of objects based on their distance from the viewer.
items.a: linear perspective [accept one-point perspective or two-point perspective; prompt on vanishing point before mention]

items.q: An artwork in this form shows a view of the city of Liege ("lee-YEZH") through the windows of a carpentry workshop. Byzantine examples of these artworks from the Romanos group include ones named for Borradaile and Harbaville made out of ivory. The Cloisters holds an artwork in this form that depicts its donors kneeling on the left as Gabriel approaches a red-clad Mary reading a book. A Giotto artwork named for Cardinal Stefaneschi shares this form with Robert Campin's Merode Altarpiece. This form was used for a painting that, when closed, depicts the creation of the world, Hieronymous Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights. For 10 points, name these artworks consisting of three panels.
items.a: triptych [prompt on polyptych; prompt on altarpiece; prompt on reliquary]

items.q: An artwork in this form depicts two vine-covered cypresses curling toward a cross adorned with five rosettes. Six medallions made with the champleve("shon-luh-VAY") technique decorate a Mosan artwork in this form that also holds two other miniature examples of this form.An artwork in this form shows a view of the city of Liege ("lee-YEZH") through the windows of a carpentry workshop. Byzantine examples of these artworks from the Romanos group include ones named for Borradaile and (*) Harbaville made out of ivory. The Cloisters hold an artwork in this form that depicts its donors kneeling on the left as Gabriel approaches a red-clad Mary reading a book. A Giotto artwork named for Cardinal Stefaneschi shares this form with Robert Campin's Merode Altarpiece. For 10 points, name these artworks consisting of three panels.
items.a: triptych [prompt on polyptych; prompt on altarpiece; prompt on reliquary] (The second clue refers to the Stavelot Triptych.)

items.q: One work in this form shows a brass band playing at a dinner party in its center. Otto Dix's Metropolis is in this form, as are many works, including one showing "Figures at the Base of a Crucifixion," by Francis Bacon. A Hugo van der Goes work for the Portinarifamily is in this form. The outer portions of artworks in this form were often done in grisaille in the Southern Netherlands, where this was the dominant form of altarpieces. They typically have a central panel and two side panels. For 10 points, name these types of artworks that are divided into three parts.
items.a: triptychs [prompt on polyptych; prompt on altarpiece]

items.q: A green-skinned Man of Sorrows appears in an Umbrian work in this format by the Master of the Borgo Crucifix. The 1992 cleaning of a work in this format revealed an island and a white castle on a small silver-leaf orb that tops a flagstaff. A blue velvet frame with pearls and 16 medallions bordered a work in this format with a Virgin Mary likely modeled on Agnes Sorel ("ahn-YESS so-REL"). Wax interiors were part of Byzantine "consular" works in this format, while an "imperial" one depicts a mounted emperor and is named for the Barberini family. Gothic works in this format include one named for Wilton House and one that Jean Fouquet painted for Melun. This format's devotional nature was adopted for a silkscreen of 50 garish, monochrome portraits from the 1953 film Niagara. For 10 points, Andy Warhol used what format to memorialize Marilyn Monroe?
items.a: diptychs [accept Marilyn Diptych, Melun Diptych, Wilton Diptych, or Barberini Diptych; prompt on polyptychs; prompt on altarpieces; prompt on panel painting or hinged; prompt on ivory by asking "in what format?"]

items.q: Note to moderator: Read the answerline carefully. Francesco Bandini names a Florentine version of this scene that unusually depicts four subjects. According to Vasari, the regret of altering the sash of an artwork depicting this scene led an artist to vow never to sign his future works. A version of this scene was created to accompany the funerary chapel of Cardinal Jean de Bilheres in Old St. Peter's Basilica. Flower-shaped wounds and red lines of paint cover an emaciated subject in a wooden version of this scene once owned by the (*) Rottgen collection. A matriarch was deliberately sculpted as youthful and oversized in a Vatican version of this scene by Michelangelo. For 10 points, name this sculptural scene depicting a lamenting Mary cradling the dead body of Jesus Christ after his deposition from the Cross.
items.a: Pieta [accept Madonna della Pieta or Vatican Pieta; accept Bandini Pieta or Florentine Pieta; accept The Deposition or The Lamentation over the Dead Christ until "Vasari" is read; prompt on lamentation of Christ until "lamenting" is read; prompt on pity or compassion]

items.q: A blue dress adorns a figure in a pre-Renaissance painted wood sculpture of this scene titled for its Southern German origin. Castilian artists Juan de Juni and Gregorio Fernandez created polychrome wooden sculptures of this scene, which were incorporated into processions called paso. An artist carved his signature onto the sash of a figure in a sculpture of this scene commissioned for Jean Bilheres de Lagraulas to prove it was not by Cristoforo Solari. A Bandini version of this scene that includes Nicodemus and Mary Magdalene was nearly destroyed in a fit of rage and is titled The Deposition. St. Peter's Basilica houses a sculpture of this scene that depicts a controversially youthful woman at Mount Golgotha who cradles the injured central figure. Michelangelo created a version of, for 10 points, what scene depicting Mary holding Jesus' dead body?
items.a: Pieta [or Lamentation of Christ; prompt on Deposition before mentioned]

items.q: This work was commissioned for the tomb of Jean de Bilheres and was carved out of a single slab of Carrara marble. Laszlo Toth attacked this work with a hammer while shouting "I am Jesus Christ," and seven sheets of plexiglass protected it while on loan at the 1964 World's Fair in New York. This sculpture has been criticized for the (*) youthful appearance of a figure who is a generation older than the other person in it, and it was moved to St. Peter's Basilica in the 18th century. For 10 points, name this Michelangelo work in which Mary holds the body of Jesus in her lap.
items.a: Pieta <TG>

items.q: It's not the Last Supper, but a black-and-white parody of this Biblical scene was photographed in 1996 by Renee Cox. Five versions of this scene were made by Gregorio Fernandez. A 2012 painting by Marlene Dumas is modeled after a sculpture of this scene that features two people standing and is known as the Rondanini version. An altar at Notre-Dame Cathedral displays a version of this scene by Nicolas Coustou. Nicodemus appears in both a Titian painting and the (*) "Florentine" version of this scene. The artist of the most famous sculpture of this scene explained the strangely youthful appearance of a woman by claiming "chaste women stay fresh." That sculpture, which has a base of rock from Golgotha, was attacked by Laszlo Toth in 1972. For 10 points, identify this Biblical scene, frequently sculpted by Michelangelo, that depicts Mary holding the dead Christ.
items.a: Pieta [prompt on Lamentation of Christ]

items.q: A member of this school, nicknamed "le grand refuse," used muted dark colors in his painting The Forest in Winter at Sunset. An artist from this school painted landscapes of the pond on his property in Ville-d'Avray and depicted the ruins of a Roman bridge in his The Bridge at Narni. This school popularized painting en plein air and its most famous member depicted a (*) praying man and woman standing in a field at dusk in his painting The Angelus. For 10 points, name this school whose members include painters Theodore Rousseau, Camille Corot, and Jean-Francois Millet, which takes its name from a village near the Forest of Fontainebleau.
items.a: Barbizon School

items.q: One member of this group was angered when his painting Moonlight was mishung by the Royal Academy. "Oxen at Work" and "Cattle Drinking" are among the characteristic paintings of another member of this group, Constant Troyon. William Morris Hunt led an American offshoot of this group, whose original version included Charles- Francois Daubigny, a man known as "le grand refuse", and a man who painted The Bridge at Narni shortly before joining it, the last of whom is Camille (*) Corot. Another member of this school painted two praying farmers in The Angelus and depicted three peasant women bending over to pick up the remnants of a grain harvest in The Gleaners. For 10 points, name this school founded by Theodore Rousseau and Jean-Francois Millet, which gathered in a namesake village near the Forest of Fontainbleau.
items.a: the Barbizon school

items.q: A composer affiliated with this visual art movement painted a ghostly, brownish face in his self-portrait, The Red Gaze. Another artist from this movement was inspired by Byzantine icons to create his Mystical Heads series. A painter from this movement wrote the sentence "And all being is flaming sorrow" on the back of a painting of a forest fire characterized by clashing (*) diagonals. Painters in this movement included Alexey von Jawlensky ("yav-LEN-skee") and an artist who analyzed the music-like effects of different colors on the psyche in Concerning the Spiritual in Art. Another artist from this movement created many zoological paintings like The Yellow Cow and The Fate of the Animals. For 10 points, name this group of Expressionist painters including Franz Marc and Wassily ("VASS-uh-lee") Kandinsky.
items.a: Der Blaue Reiter [or the Blue Rider; prompt on German Expressionism before it is read]

items.q: An artist from this movement painted a pale blue figure gazing at the viewer in his work Astonishment. Paintings of colorful female heads in this movement's style were created by its member Alexei von Jawlensky [yah-VLEN-skee]. Paul Klee restored a painting from this movement that depicts a blue deer twisting and looking straight up amidst chaos. Its founder argued different orientations of lines produce different effects and tonalities in his book Point and Line to Plane. The artist of (*) The Fate of the Animals was part of this movement, as was a man who analyzed the effect of color on the soul in On the Spiritual in Art and painted a series of increasingly abstract works simply titled "Compositions." For 10 points, name this art movement that was named after a painting by Wassily Kandinsky.
items.a: Der Blaue Reiter [ or The Blue Rider]

items.q: A member of this group depicted an oarsman wearing only red briefs in Three Girls in a Barque. A successor to this group founded by Galka Scheyer included the Russian painter Alexey von Jawlensky. One member of this group demonstrated principles like "red is matter, brutal and heavy" in a painting whose title creatures are trapped in a vague apocalyptic event. Its founder argued that one's inner spirit should inform the color of a canvas in On the (*) Spiritual in Art, and its namesake Almanac included contributions from the painter of The Fate of the Animals. Its members included August Macke and Franz Marc. For 10 points, identify this art movement named for a Wassily Kandinsky painting of a cloaked figure atop a white horse.
items.a: Der Blaue Reiter [or The Blue Rider]

items.q: One member of this movement depicted another member painting in front of a gate and a village; the latter artist painted a boy seated at a table looking out a window at some snow-covered trees in Breakfast of the Birds. An 18th century couple on a balcony appears in Rokoko, a work from this movement by an artist who painted faceless children in Farewell and some naked women with a turbaned pilot in Three Girls in a Barque. This movement was founded after Angel of the Last Judgement was rejected at a salon. Another member of this group included (*) boars, foxes, and a deer in his Fate of the Animals. Gabriele Munter and August Macke belonged to this movement, which was founded by the author of On the Spiritual in Art. For 10 points, name this group co-founded by Franz Marc and named for a figure in a green field painted by its member Wassily Kandinsky.
items.a: Der Blaue Reiter (or The Blue Rider)

items.q: An artist who worked in this style visited Egypt and copied a Seurat bridge painting as inspiration for color works like Gala and Shadow Play. Richard Anuszkiewicz's ("ah-noosh-k'YAY-vich's") Translumina series exemplifies this non-French style. It's not minimalism, but Donald Judd coined this style's name in a Time review of a Julian Stanczak ("STAHN-chak") exhibition. Paintings in this style motivated by "planetary folklore" were featured at an exhibition called The Responsive (*) Eye. A painting in this style depicts the interlocking limbs of two zebras. Grids of black-and-white squares attenuate as they meet in a painting in this style, Movement in Squares. Contrasting colors that create the appearance of depth are featured in works in this style by Victor Vasarely and Bridget Riley. For 10 points, works in what 20th-century artistic style often create feelings of dizziness via visual illusions?
items.a: op art [or optical art; accept optical illusions; accept opto-kinetic art; prompt on kinetic art; prompt on abstract art] (The painter in the lead-in is Bridget Riley. Victor Vasarely developed the idea of "planetary folklore.")

items.q: In 1964, a Julian Stanczak show at the Martha Jackson gallery prompted Time magazine to coin the name of which style of art? Works in this style include Nataraja, a canvas of coloured diamonds, and Blaze, a black-and-white series of nested circles created by bent lines, both of which are by Bridget Riley. 1965's The Responsive Eye was an early and very popular exhibition of this style, based on visual effect.
items.a: op art (or optical art)

items.q: The "blind romanticization" of this movement is critiqued in Cauleen Smith's Remote Viewing. Judy Chicago countered this movement's masculinity with a series of ephemeral, colorful performances, featuring her students nude with body paint. Phil Leider described going with Abbie Hoffman to see a work from this movement, Michael Heizer's Double Negative. A work from this movement was installed at (*) Kent State University in 1970 to depict the effects of "entropy." Kanye West filmed Jesus Is King at a site for art of this type by James Turrell. The University of Michigan campus is the site of Wave Field, Maya Lin's piece of this type. At Rozel Point, Robert Smithson created a piece of this type by moving over 6,000 tons of basalt. For 10 points, Spiral Jetty is part of what movement that engages directly with the Earth?
items.a: land art [or environmental art; accept Earth art BEFORE the final word; prompt on sculptures; prompt on installation art; prompt on site-specific art; prompt on Light and Space with "what larger artistic movement is that Turrell site part of?"] (Remote Viewing responds to Partially Buried Woodshed. The Judy Chicago piece is Atmospheres. The James Turrell site is Roden Crater.)

items.q: In 2020, a sculpture in this medium, located at the Presidio Golf Club, was found to have been set on fire. Vik Muniz famously photographed works in this medium, including depictions of keys and paper clips. A work in this medium was the subject of a 30 minute long documentary film shot by its artist and his wife, Nancy Holt. It's not a skyscape, but James Turrell has been working on an artwork in this medium since 1979. Alan Sonfist created (*) Time Landscape as a part of an art movement centered around this medium. One artist in this medium, formerly a professor of applied mathematics, created works like Cairn and Spire. For 10 points, name this common medium of Andy Goldsworthy and Robert Smithson, who created works like Spiral Jetty.
items.a: land art [accept earth art; accept the Earthworks movement]

items.q: Described as a "gateway to observe light, time and space," and located in the Arizona desert, Roden Crater is an artwork belonging to which movement? The most famous work of this movement was built on the shore of the Great Salt Lake by Robert Smithson, and is named Spiral Jetty.
items.a: Land Art (or Earth Art or Earthworks or Environmental Art)

items.q: The essay "An Account from My Hut" laments the whirlwind, fire, and earthquake that struck this city, and also recounts six months when it lost its status as the capital. After this city's construction, the meaning of the province containing it changed from "mountain back" to "mountain castle." The enthronement of Komyo in this city led to the creation of a puppet (*) Northern Court. Due to the wariness of Buddhist influence following an attempted coup during the Nara period, only two temples were allowed in this city, right next to the Rashomon gate. This city names a period of history during which Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, and that period was succeeded by the Kamakura Shogunate. For 10 points, before Tokyo, what city was the capital of Japan?
items.a: Kyoto [or Heian-kyo]

items.q: Since 2013 this city has mandated that most metal walls be black or gray and that companies use muted colors in their logos, to preserve its overall aesthetics. This city contains a moss garden arranged circularly around a "golden pond," as well as fifteen rocks in a "dry landscape" arranged so they cannot all be seen at once from the ground. A temple in this city was deliberately left incomplete after its commissioning ruler died, but its name reflects the ruler's plan to (*) coat its roof with foil. At a shrine in this city, lanterns hang from 800 red gates which are packed together, resembling a tunnel. A temple in this city with gilded walls burned down in 1950. For 10 points, name this city whose medieval buildings, such as the Temple of the Golden Pavilion, reflect its heritage as Japan's old capital.
items.a: Kyoto

items.q: This city was the site of the Hamaguri Gate Rebellion, also called the Kinmon Incident. Emperor Kanmu moved his capital from Nara to the Daidairi Palace in this city, beginning the Heian Period. The Battle of Toba-Fushimi occurred in a field between this city and Osaka. Following the Battle of Sekigahara, Shogun Tokugawa moved his capital from this city to Edo. For the point, name this cultural capital of Japan, replaced as the seat of government in 1603 by Tokyo.
items.a: Kyoto (accept Heian-kyo)

items.q: A politician from this city commented on the increasing reliance of men on their wives' male relatives due to the emerging trend of uxorilocal marriages with the quote, "A man's wife makes him who he is." The Mayfly Diary was written to counter romantic tales of life in this city. A bureaucrat known for his romantic affairs in this city was the most prolific of a group of six literary "geniuses" and likely inspired the creation of the irogonomi. Residents of this city were the most powerful beneficiaries of a system sometimes called onnade exemplified by the (*) Iroha poem; that poem and the kana system were allegedly created here by Kukai. Potentially rival courts developed in this city around Empresses Teishi and Shoshi, the former of whom patronized Sei Shonagon. For 10 points, name this city, whose courtly life is explored in The Pillow Book and The Tale of Genji.
items.a: Kyoto [accept Heian-kyo]

items.q: The world's second-largest aquarium tank is in this city, where an oblong-shaped bright yellow Ferris wheel depicting a deity holding a penguin was recently renovated by the retail chain Don Quijote. One of this city's mascots is a mechanical drum-playing clown named after this city's culture of "eat till you drop," while others include a giant mechanical crab and a running man on a Glico billboard. A crowd in this city seeking a Randy Bass lookalike chose a Colonel Sanders statue to throw into a river, leading to a curse on the Hanshin Tigers. This city's tourist destinations include the entertainment district Dotonbori and a castle owned by the Toyotomi clan that was besieged by Ieyasu Tokugawa. The Keihanshin metropolitan area is formed by Kobe, Kyoto, and, for 10 points, what city in the Kansai region, which after Tokyo and Yokohama is the third most populous in Japan?
items.a: Osaka [or Osaka-shi]

items.q: One battle in this city resulted in the moat of a castle being filled in after the invading army could not breach Sanada Maru. A summer offensive in this city succeeded following victories for the invaders at the battles of Wakae (WA-KA-EH) and the Battle of Yao. That offensive in this city killed Sanada Yukimura at the (*) Battle of Tennoji, causing Toyotomi Hideyori to commit seppuku. This city was the site of a 1615 siege and burning of its namesake castle that effectively ended the Sengoku period. For 10 points, name this third largest city in Japan.
items.a: Osaka

items.q: While working in this city, the leader of the Ewo group made extensive investments in America managed by railroad magnate John Murray Forbes. That man renowned among Americans took on the name Howqua while working in this city. Exorbitant fees for entering this city could be set by an official called Hoppo responsible directly to his ruler. The Consoo fund was raised with levies charged in this city to cover debts incurred by bankruptcies.
