According to legend, a Gilbert Stuart painting was saved from this building by Dolley Madison after it was burned by the British during the War of 1812. For 10 points, name this building on 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, where the American president lives.
items.a: The White House

items.q: The commissioner of this building picked its architect after seeing his work on the Charleston County Courthouse. Louis Comfort Tiffany modified it by adorning its entrance hall with a massive multi-colored glass screen, which was taken out in 1902 when Charles McKim renovated the whole building. This building was modeled after the Leinster House by its original architect, who used a modified version of north and south porticos designed by B.H. Latrobe when he rebuilt it after a fire. It was built by James Hoban, who won five hundred dollars in a design competition. Rooms in this building include the Blue Room, the Map Room, and the Cabinet Room, which overlooks the Rose Garden. For 10 points, name this residence which also contains the Oval Office.
items.a: The White House

items.q: The location for this memorial was a former World War I-era Munitions building that had been demolished. Early opposition to this memorial came from James Webb, who called it a "nihilistic (*) slab of stone," and the then-Secretary of the Interior initially refused to issue a building permit for it. For 10 points, name this memorial, created for an art class at Yale University, in Washington D.C. that contains two walls sunk into the ground at a right angle, that commemorates over 58,000 dead from the title conflict, designed by Maya Lin.
items.a: The Vietnam Veterans' Memorial (accept "Vietnam Wall" and "Vietnam War Memorial")

items.q: Chris Burden created an "Other" version of this artwork, while Diane Carlson Evans raised funds for a women's version of it. 287 additions were made to this work after its completion, and Duery Felton, Jr. organized a collection of objects left next to it. Viewers must walk down a slight grade to approach this work, whose two main components combine to form a "V" shape and are made from gabbro. The artist later created a similar sculpture for (*) Montgomery, Alabama's Civil Rights Museum. This sculpture is accompanied by Frederick Hart's The Three Soldiers. During its construction, a Purple Heart was thrown into the concrete foundation. For 10 points, name this Maya Lin-designed memorial to American soldiers killed in an Asian conflict.
items.a: Vietnam Veterans Memorial [or Vietnam Wall or Vietnam War Memorial]

items.q: This object inspires the thought that "My clouded reflection eyes me like a bird of prey" in the Yusef Komunyakaa poem "Facing It." The creation of this work is the subject of the documentary A Strong, Clear Vision. It is complemented by a bronze group depicting three white, black, and Hispanic men designed by Frederick Hart. The design of this (*) V-shaped sculpture was selected from over a thousand submissions by a panel that settled on the idea of a 21-year-old Asian-American Yale student. For 10 points, name this memorial designed by Maya Lin and consisting of a black wall with over 50,000 names.
items.a: the Vietnam Veterans' Memorial [prompt on Vietnam Memorial or other partial answers; do not accept or prompt on "Vietnam War Memorial"]

items.q: There are two half-sized replicas of this work currently traveling; one first went on display in 1984 in Tyler, Texas, and the other debuted in 1996. Those are the "moving" one and the one "that heals", respectively. One sculptural addition to the main part of this was so offensive to the architect of the main element that the architect refused to attend its dedication. That Frederick Hart sculpture is of three men who are Caucasian, Asian, and Hispanic. Another addition featured Hope, Faith, and Charity, three nurses tending to a wounded soldier. The main part of this work is an organic design of two gabbro walls sunk into the earth that tapered down at the ends. With over 58,000 names engraved in its walls, for 10 points, identify this work that was designed by then-Yale undergraduate Maya Lin.
items.a: Vietnam Veterans Memorial

items.q: This artist criticized another artist's crucifix as depicting a "peasant on the cross," prompting him to create a crucifix now displayed in the Gondi Chapel. A creation by this artist was intended to carry marble and was called the "sea-going monster," or Il Badalone. A design by this artist was demonstrated when he balanced a cracked egg on its point. Andrea della Robbia designed reliefs of babies for a building he designed, the Hospital of the Innocents. This artist used a herringbone brick pattern for an octagonal structure built on top of the Santa Maria del Fiore, created after losing a contest to Lorenzo Ghiberti. For 10 points, name this Italian artist who designed the dome of the Florence Cathedral.
items.a: Filippo Brunelleschi

items.q: Workers under this artist used a terracotta pot to create peposo stew during a project for which this artist created a marble transportation ship that sank on its maiden voyage. This artist died before a lantern he designed could be topped by a golden ball and cross designed by Andrea del Verrocchio. Andrea della Robbia created a series of blue tondi decorated with babies for this artist's construction of the Ospedale degli Innocenti. This artist used stone and chain hoops to connect the inner and outer walls of a herringbone-patterned brick building. After losing a contest to design a city's baptistery doors to Lorenzo Ghiberti, this artist constructed an octagonal building without flying buttresses. For 10 points, name this Renaissance architect who created the dome for the Florence Cathedral.
items.a: Filippo Brunelleschi

items.q: After his death, a rotating wheel was placed in the portico of an orphanage designed by this person. This person omitted the need for scaffolding by using a herringbone brick pattern in a work topped by a posthumously completed lantern. In one experiment, this person viewed a mirror through a tiny hole in a painting, thus rediscovering linear perspective. This (*) architect used a double-layered design for an octagonal brick structure that sits atop the Santa Maria del Fiore without the need for Flying Buttresses. For 10 points, name this Renaissance architect of the duomo of the Florence Cathedral.
items.a: Filippo Brunelleschi [prompt on Pippo]

items.q: This man is credited with the first system of linear perspective and designed an arcade with nine arches for a hospital in Florence. This man, who built a sacristy with white walls for the Basilica of San Lorenzo, designed an eight-sided rotunda for the Santa Maria degli Angeli ("DAY-lee an-JEL-ly") and did (moderator note: emphasis) not design the bronze (*) doors to the Florence baptistry because he lost a contest to Lorenzo Ghiberti ("ghee-BARE-tee"). Donatello designed a brick miniature of this man's most famous work, which consisted of an outer and inner layer. For 10 points, name this Italian architect who designed the dome of the Florence Cathedral.
items.a: Filippo Brunelleschi

items.q: This author wrote a text whose second book opens by retelling the story of Narcissus gazing at his own reflection to compare his own profession with "embracing" the "surface of the pool." Anthony Grafton's book about this author discusses his tendency to "personalize" his "ancient sources" in his written works, such as one in which this author cites the story of a cobbler antagonizing Alexander the Great's personal portraitist. This man suggested that artists populate their works with a "variety of things" so that the "soul of the viewer" will be moved through a narrative mode called historia. He was inspired by Vitruvius to write De Re Aedificatoria, a ten-book treatise on architecture. This architect designed the facade for the Santa Maria Novella, and he wrote a 1435 book that was the first to suggest that artists use a vanishing point to create illusionistic perspective. For 10 points, what Florentine architect wrote the first post-classical treatise on painting, Della Pittura?
items.a: Leon Battista Alberti

items.q: In a painting by this person, a window overlooking ships and a distant landscape is behind a ringletted Christ tied to an elaborately foliated column. In Milan, this person designed the sixteen-sided dome of Santa Maria delle Grazie, and produced another painting in which a trompe-l'œil makes an alcove seem to be an entire choir around the altar of Santa Maria presso San Satiro. Ferdinand and Isabella commissioned this person to design a monument on the site of St Peter's (*) crucifixion, for which they built a perfectly circular building. A dome designed by this person was revised into an ovoid by Michelangelo, while a neighbouring building contains a double-helix staircase named for this person and commissioned by Pope Julius II. For 10 points, name this architect of the Tempietto, the first architect of the modern St Peter's Basilica in Rome.
items.a: Donato Bramante [or Donato di Pascuccio d'Antonio]

items.q: One work originally attributed to this architect is now thought to have been mainly designed by Giovanni Antonio Amadeo. This architect designed a palazzo which was demolished in the 17th century, but earlier served as a residence for Raphael. His namesake cloister is located in the Santa Maria della Pace, and he is widely credited with designing the apse of the Santa Maria della (*) Grazie. He designed a small but harmonious building in the courtyard of the church of San Pietro in Montorio, meant to commemorate the location of St. Peter's martyrdom. This architect of the Tempietto is best known for a design based on a Greek cross with a dome based on the Pantheon, but he was replaced by Sangallo, Fra Giocondo and Raphael when his patron Julius II died. For 10 points, name this architect who was the original designer of St. Peter's Basilica.
items.a: Donato Bramante

items.q: His early career was spent painting, producing poorly preserved works in the Casa Prinetti and Casa Fontana. After becoming court architect for Lodovico Sforza, he designed the choir and transept of the Santa Maria della Grazie and the Canonica of San Ambrogio. One of his last projects was the extension of the Vatican Belvedere as two long, parallel structures. The influence of Leonardo can be seen in the radial design, including a cylindrical cella surrounded by a circular peristyle, of a shrine on the site where St. Peter was crucified. His most monumental design employed a Greek cross with four equal arms and a large hemishpheric dome. FTP, name this favorite architect of Julius II; the creator of the Tempietto and the original designer of St. Peter's Basilica.
items.a: Donato Bramante

items.q: Inigo Jones's Banqueting House at Whitehall was inspired by this architect's work, whose common name was given to him by an early patron, Trissino. This architect designed the Teatro Olimpico in Vicenza, which features a UNESCO site named for his (*) villas in the Venuto. This man's Church of San Giorgio Maggiore was being built at the time of the publishing of his The Four Books of Architecture. For 10 points, name this Italian architect of the Villa Rotonda.
items.a: Andrea Palladio [accept Andrea di Pietro della Gondola] <TG>

items.q: A house designed by this man includes two symmetrical wings leading out to pavilions that sport sundials underneath the pediments of their facades. After his death, a theater designed by this man was given a trompe-l'œil set designed to look like a long street heading upstage. A church designed by this man uses white marble for a four-column, elevated classical temple facade that's superimposed over a second, lower temple facade. A country house designed by this man has (*) porticos facing each of the four cardinal directions. This designer of the Olympic Theater adapted Roman temple designs for his many villas in and around Vicenza. Monticello was built on principles inspired by this designer of San Giorgio Maggiore. For 10 points, name this Venetian Renaissance architect who wrote the Four Books on Architecture and designed the Villa Rotonda.
items.a: Andrea Palladio [or Andrea di Pietro]

items.q: This architect's final design for the Teatro Olimpico was not completed until after his death, and the bell tower of his Church of San Giorgio Maggiore collapsed in 1774. This architect worked as a mason on the Villa Trissino and used principles of design by (*) Vitruvius in most of his villas and palaces. For 10 points, name this Italian author of Four Books of Architecture and designer of the Villa Rotonda.
items.a: Andrea Palladio

items.q: This man included a long wing ending in a series of dovecotes for a Bagnolo building; that structure also includes a barrel-vaulted main room. One building designed by this man includes frescoes by Battista Franco and was nicknamed "La Malcontenta," his Villa Foscari. He also designed an edifice whose bell tower collapsed in 1774, the Church of San Giorgio Maggiore. One of this man's most famous structures is a dome whose design was altered by his fellow architect Scamozzi after his death. That villa contains a large central dome. For 10 points, name this architect of the Villa Rotunda who wrote the Four Books of Architecture.
items.a: Andrea Palladio

items.q: This sculptor created a mattress for a Roman sculpture discovered at the Santa Maria della Vittoria. An unfinished sculpture by this artist depicts a woman holding the Sun while standing on the Earth. Sculptures of the Cornaro family occupy a balcony and watch over this artist's depiction of a "dart of love." This artist's several works for the Borghese Gallery include one of Pluto carrying away Prosperina and another of Daphne turning into a tree. This sculptor of Truth Unveiled by Time depicted golden rays falling on an angel as he prepares to thrust his spear into a nun. For 10 points, name this Italian Baroque sculptor of The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa.
items.a: Gian Lorenzo Bernini

items.q: John Evlyn's diaries described how this artist designed special effects in which a theater caught fire, but transformed into a garden. This artist was inspired by Stromboli's eruption to design the first annual fireworks display at the Castel Sant'Angelo. In a tomb designed by this artist, a billowing jasper cloak traps a skeleton who holds an hourglass. This artist placed putti above a lay woman who reclines on a pillow and grasps her heart in a sculpture for the (*) Altieri Chapel depicting Ludovica Albertoni. At age 81, this artist finished the tomb of Alexander VII. Portraits of donors in theater boxes flank a sculpture by this artist in the Cornaro Chapel which shows an angel standing over a woman on a cloud. For 10 points, name this sculptor who depicted an arrow pointed at a nun in The Ecstasy of St. Theresa.
items.a: Gian Lorenzo Bernini

items.q: The Trastevere district of one city contains this man's depiction of a local mystic, Blessed Ludovica Albertoni . A bronze dove tops a sculpture by this artist which centers on an Egyptian obelisk. A two-figure work by this artist is located in the Santa Maria della Vittoria's Cornaro Chapel, while Rome's (*) Piazza Navona is home to his allegory of the Danube, Nile, Ganges, and Rio de la Plata. This sculptor of the Fountain ofthe Four Rivers is best known for a depiction of a Spanish saint being euphorically pierced by an angel's spear. For 10 points, name this Italian sculptor of The Ecstasy of St. Theresa.
items.a: Gian Lorenzo Bernini

items.q: One of this artist's unfinished works depicts a nude woman holding a face representing the sun, and was originally supposed to depict Time disrobing her. Death raises an hourglass in a tomb by this artist, which shows Truth putting their foot on England on a globe to represent Alexander VII ("the seventh") subduing Anglicanism. An Egyptian obelisk with the Pamphili (pam-FEE-lee) family emblem appears behind gods representing the (*) Rio de la Plata, Nile, Danube, and Ganges in this artist's Fountain of the Four Rivers. Another of their works stands in the Santa Maria della Vittoria's Cornaro Chapel and depicts an angel pointing an arrow at a swooning nun. For 10 points, name this Baroque sculptor of The Ecstasy of St. Theresa.
items.a: Gian Lorenzo Bernini

items.q: An early work by this artist found at the Vatican was a mountain-shaped fountain with five bees which serve as spouts, the Fontana delle Api. This artist mounted icosahedra onto shortened double-scroll volutes that he borrowed from Michelangelo's Porta Pia atop an altar in Naples's Church of Santi Apostoli, the Filomarino Altar. The floor plan of a church by this artist consists of a hexagon formed in a six-pointed stars, with the points alternately replaced by circles or concavities. This artist reused that Porta Pia motif on the piers of the buttresses of a dome he designed for that church which is topped by a lantern featuring a spiral ramp leading up to a globe and cross. The facade of a church designed by this architect for the Spanish Trinitarians in Rome features a pattern of concavities and convex projections in the form of a double-S curve. For 10 points, name this architect of the Church of St. Ivo della Sapienza and the Church of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane.
items.a: Francesco Borromini

items.q: The floorplan of a building designed by this man consists of an equilateral triangle with a semicircle added to each side and a sector cut out from each corner. For his first independent commission, he designed a building around a pre-existing fountain featuring the River Tiber sitting under an oak tree next to a she-wolf. This nephew of Carlo Maderno worked on the Sant'Agnese in Agone, whose position on the Piazza Navona led to an urban legend that the figure of the Nile in the Fountain of the Four Rivers raises his hand to shield himself against its ugliness. This architect designed a building whose dome is tessellated with octagonal, hexagonal, and cross-shaped coffers surrounding a dove hovering below the lantern. He placed a corkscrew lantern atop his design for Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza. For 10 points, name this Italian Baroque architect of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, who loved undulating walls and ovals and hated Bernini.
items.a: Francesco Borromini

items.q: This man was a Savilian Professor of Astronomy at Oxford and was a founding member of the Royal Society. Additionally, this man rejected a request from King Charles II to direct the construction of fortifications near Tangier. This architect designed a 201-foot Doric column as a monument to one event. With Jonas Moore, designed the (*) Royal Greenwich Observatory. This man's tombstone is inscribed with "If you seek his memorial, Look around you." For 10 points, name this English architect who rebuilt many churches in London after the Great Fire and designed St. Paul's Cathedral.
items.a: Christopher Wren

items.q: This man was inspired by the Roman Theater of Marcellus for his design of the Sheldonian Theater. This architect designed a 202-foot column known as "The Monument," and, along with William Talman, redesigned the Hampton Court Palace for (*) William and Mary. This architect designed the Royal Observatory at Greenwich and rebuilt 52 churches after the Great Fire of London, including one located at the top of Ludgate Hill. For 10 points, name this architect of St Paul's Cathedral.
items.a: Christopher Wren

items.q: This man illustrated the book that introduced the word "neurology". This man inspired the design of the Provincetown Heritage Museum, which appears in a Charles Demuth painting titled After this man. The illustrations for Thomas Willis's Cerebri Anatome were created by this man, who lamented "ladies think nothing well without an edging." This namesake of the oldest building on the campus of William & Mary took on Nicholas (*) Hawksmoor as an apprentice. This architect designed the library of Trinity College Cambridge and the Old Royal Naval College in Greenwich. For 10 points, name this architect whose 54 London churches include St Paul's Cathedral.
items.a: Christopher Wren

items.q: This man's three story transparent version was the first recorded observation beehive, and he designed one of the first wooden box beehives. A building at William & Mary University designed by this man is the oldest known collegiate building in America. As City Surveyor, Robert Hooke worked with this builder to design the (*) Greenwich Royal Observatory, as well as a 202-foot column memorializing the Great Fire of London. For 10 points, name this architect who designed St. Paul's Cathedral.
items.a: Christopher Wren

items.q: Fiona MacCarthy's biography of this artist tells how on their deathbed a physician diagnosed them with "simply being [this artist]." This artist designed a revivalist serif font called the Golden Type for an edition of Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend. John Henry Dearle and Lucy Faulkner Orrinsmith helped this artist develop an aesthetic used for "Larkspur" and "Strawberry Thief." Long before Tolkien, this artist included a horse named Silverfax and a character named Gandolf in the (+) fantasy novel The Well at the World's End. This artist founded a publishing house that produced a lavish 1896 edition of Chaucer with illustrations by Edward Burne-Jones. Besides the Kelmscott Press, this anarchist ran a firm with several pre-Raphaelites that promoted a handmade, medieval aesthetic of (*) decoration. For 10 points, name this prolific designer of wallpaper and textiles who founded the British Arts and Crafts movement.
items.a: William Morris

items.q: This artist was told upon graduation, "We awarded a diploma to a madman or a genius. Time will tell". Although currently deceased, this artist's most famous work is not expected to be completed until 2026. This (*) architect's work is marked by walls and structures that express circular movement, complemented by colorful mosaics and stained glass windows. Many of this artist's projects bear the name of Eusebi Guell ("ooh-seh-bee gwel"), who funded most of this architect's projects. This architect's works include Casa Battlo ("bat-low"), Guell Palace, and Casa Mila. For ten points, name this Spanish architect known for the gothic revival cathedral, Sagrada Familia.
items.a: Antoni Gaudi

items.q: The roof of one of this man's buildings is arched and tiled to resemble a dragon, and the front facade of that building exemplifies his use of trencadis. His last commissioned work features 28 twisted chimneys in addition to a self-supporting, undulating stone facade. Those works are the Casa Batllo and the Casa Mila. Many of his projects were funded by his patron Eusebi (*) Guell, including a park whose entrance features a famous mosaic-tiled salamander. The Nativity facade of his most famous work bears the most direct influence from him. For 10 points, name this Spanish Catalan architect of the unfinished Sagrada Familia.
items.a: Antoni Gaudi <FK>

items.q: A house by this architect was posthumously built by Graham Roxburgh ("ROCKS-bruh")despite being disqualified from a German design competition due to a late entry. This man designed a series of high-backed chairs for the premises of Catherine Cranston. This architect's house for the publisher Walter Blackie features a Portland cement exterior with gessoes in the interior designed by his wife. This architect, who designed the (*) House for an Art Lover, names a building he designed for his alma mater in Garnethill. The National Trust have since put a chainmail mesh box around this architect's Hill House to help it to dry off. After reopening in 2018, this architect's name was appended to the name of the Willow Tearooms, which he designed in 1903. For 10 points, name this British Art Nouveau architect who designed part of the Glasgow School of Art.
items.a: Charles Rennie Mackintosh [accept Mackintosh at the Willow]

items.q: This architect's quote "art is the flower - life is the green leaf" is often paired with sketches of roses, which this architect often paired with teardrops in designs. This architect designed a "kimono desk" and requested North American yellow pine to build a gallery of dark timber beams and columns for a library modeled on Japanese interiors. A stylized swallow decorates the high back of a series of chairs by this architect which were commissioned by Catherine Cranston and shown at the (*) 1900 Vienna Secession Exhibition. This architect of the Argyle Chair collaborated with his wife Margaret Macdonald on a business named for Miss Cranston. A 2018 retrospective of this artist at the Kelvingrove Art Gallery was cancelled after a fire badly damaged the library that this architect designed for an art school. For 10 points, name this architect of the Art Nouveau Willow Tea Rooms and the Glasgow School of Art.
items.a: Charles Rennie Mackintosh

items.q: A posthumously-constructed building by this architect features a long, narrow music room with small cube-shaped lamps bearing a heart motif. In 2019, a box was installed around a house this architect built for the publisher Walter Blackie to protect the Portland cement harling on its exterior walls. One of this architect's buildings features a gesso panel inspired by a Rossetti sonnet designed by his wife Margaret, an influential decorative artist. In addition to Home for an Art Lover and Hill House, this architect designed the lavish "Salon de Luxe" for one of his buildings, in which he surrounded silver-painted (*) tables with his trademark high-backed chairs. This architect was inspired by traditional Japanese woodwork to design a complex timber library for his alma mater. For 10 points, name this Scottish architect and designer, who constructed the Willow Tearooms and the Glasgow School of Art.
items.a: Charles Rennie Mackintosh <MS>

items.q: This architect's book Autobiography of an Idea ends with a description of a series of concentric arches called the Golden Door. A tripartite building now named for this architect was the first to feature large windows flanked by double hung windows and a rounded, cast-iron entrance. This architect frequently used Syrian arches and entwined Celtic patterns, the latter of which appears interlaced with bull's eye windows on a brewery office building. Buffalo's (*) Guaranty Building uses terracotta to replace the brick that Dankmar Adler and this architect used for a steel-framed skyscraper. Frank Lloyd Wright was an apprentice under, for 10 points, what architect of the Wainwright Building who used the mantra "form follows function?"
items.a: Louis Sullivan [or Louis Henry Sullivan; accept Sullivan Center]

items.q: Towards the end of this architect's career, he built banks such as the National Farmers Bank in Minnesota and Peoples Savings Bank in Iowa, which became known as his "Jewel Boxes." At the start of this architect's career, he collaborated with a German architect on a design for an Auditorium Building. A revolutionary (*) 10-story building in St. Louis was designed by this architect and Dankmar Adler. For 10 points name this architect who designed the Wainwright building and mentored Frank Lloyd Wright.
items.a: Louis Sullivan

items.q: This architect used a gold leaf style for a building prominently featuring a foil-covered Golden Door. This architect of the Transport Building for the Chicago World's Fair featured bull's-eye windows in the cornice of a different building. Later, this architect used terra cotta in his window lines to create the National Farmers Bank, one of his many so-called "jewel boxes." This architect's work with the "engineer's aesthetic" inspired his (*) Guaranty Building for Buffalo, New York. A 10-story brick collaboration between this architect and Dankmar Adler was considered one of the first skyscrapers. For 10 points, name this architect of St. Louis's Wainwright Building whose mantra was "form follows function."
items.a: Louis Sullivan

items.q: One of this architect's designs uses a slanted mastaba topped by a tower with a stepped pyramid. That Egyptian Revival style tomb for Martin Ryerson is located in Graceland Cemetary, the same location as this architect's bronze-gated Carrie Eliza Getty Tomb. This architect protested the classical style of the White City, a competitor to the gold-leaf Golden Door of his entry to the Columbian Exposition, the (*) Transportation Building. One building by this man contains murals and stained glass depictions of rural life, the National Farmers' Bank, which is one of his namesake "Jewel Boxes". This architect's most famous building features "celery-leaf" ornamentation, and is considered to be a twin to his later Guaranty Building. For 10 points, name this architect of the Wainwright Building in St. Louis, who is best known for the phrase "form follows function".
items.a: Louis Sullivan

items.q: This architect's only completed skyscraper, Price Tower, features geometric furniture designed by this architect, who based his studio Taliesin West in the Arizona desert. This architect built affordable homes in the (*) Usonian style. This architect's Imperial Hotel built in Tokyo survived an earthquake, and his Prairie-style homes, such as the Robie House, make strong use of cantilevers. For 10 points, identify this American architect of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum and Fallingwater.
items.a: Frank Lloyd Wright

items.q: This architect utilized a copper roof and hexagonal skylights in a house built for the Hagan family, and he later put his signature on a Cherokee red-colored tile on the sandstone exterior of that house, Kentuck Knob. This architect's Unity Temple is one of several buildings he designed in Oak Park, Illinois. This architect designed the (*) Johnson Wax Headquarters while working at Taliesen ("tah-lee-ESS-en"). This practitioner of organic architecture utilized light brown reinforced concrete cantilevered terraces in a house designed for the Kaufmann family. For 10 points, a waterfall on Bear Run in Pennsylvania is the site of what architect's Fallingwater?
items.a: Frank Lloyd Wright

items.q: One of this architect's early works was an office building for the Larkin Soap Company in Buffalo. This architect's mistress was murdered by Julian Carlton in a studio that he designed, which prompted him to build another "West" version of that building in Scottsdale. This architect of Taliesin ("tah-lee-AY-sin") designed a hotel that survived the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake. One of this architect's buildings was nicknamed "rising mildew" due to the water damage it sustained, and that work utilized a cantilever design to perch a building over a waterfall on Bear Run creek. For 10 points, name this American architect, who designed the house Fallingwater.
items.a: Frank Lloyd Wright

items.q: A semicircular building this architect called "his little gem" is the only one he deliberately made wheelchair accessible. This architect encouraged clients to help make the concrete blocks that formed their so-called "automatic" buildings. At age 86, this architect designed a building whose red copper and cypress roof features hexagonal skylights, and which includes a wall-less parking area. This architect claimed Samuel Butler coined a term they used for buildings that often featured (*) "carports". This architect kept the price below 5,000 dollars while designing one-story L-shaped buildings like the Jacobs House and Kentuck Knob, which exemplify their modest "Usonian homes". A house this architect designed for Edgar Kaufmann uses cantilevers to bridge the Bear Run river. For 10 points, name this architect of Fallingwater.
items.a: Frank Lloyd  Wright

items.q: This architect used internal "streets" in a typology of housing units that he co-designed and created with Nadir Afonso. In a design for a chapel, this architect designed a unique flowing curved roof, which forms part of a set of 17 sites that became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. This architect used three concrete slabs supported by six concrete columns in his open-plan Dom-ino House. Ribbon windows, free plans and gentle (*) ramps are among this architect's Five Points of Modern Architecture. This architect used his ville radieuse design concept in works in the city of Chandigarh. This architect declared "a house is a machine to live in" in his first book Towards an Architecture. For 10 points, name this French-Swiss architect of the Villa La Roche and Villa Savoye.
items.a: Le Corbusier [accept Charles-Edouard Jeanneret]

items.q: A building by this architect contains a lobby with "harsh, angular forms" and an auditorium with "soft, curvilinear forms", which this architect described as "both needing the other in order to exist". The Mill Owners' Association in Ahmedabad features this architect's "sun-breakers". This architect removed Amedee Ozenfant's contributions from articles advancing their theory of the "architectural (*) promenade". This architect declared that "staircases separate one floor from another; ramps connect them". This architect's characteristic features include the roof garden, ribbon window and pilotis. For 10 points, buildings throughout the city of Chandigarh were designed by what Swiss-French architect using their "five points of architecture"?
items.a: Le Corbusier [accept Charles-Edouard Jeanneret-Gris]

items.q: In order to study the ability to adjust sunlight in the four corners of a building, this architect designed the Tower of Shadows. This architect wrote "The End of a World" on a sketch of a multi-colored sculpture that can be rotated by the wind. Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew worked with this architect and his cousin on a project for which he designed the Palace of Assembly and the Secretariat Building. The golden ratio and the human form inspired much of this architect's (*) Modulor system. This architect designed the Open Hand Monument for a planned city based on his ideal "Radiant City." The city of Chandigarh incorporates the "five points," such as free design of facades, as outlined in this architect's Towards a New Architecture. For 10 points, name this Swiss-French architect of the Villa Savoye.
items.a: Le Corbusier [or Charles-Edouard Jeanneret-Gris]

items.q: In one book by this author titled When the Cathedrals were White, he discusses the influence of color on New Yorkers. Many of this author's works were published in his magazine L'Esprit Nouveau . Heating problems and rain leakage stemmed from ideas of this author like lengthy horizontal (*) windows and a flat roof. A nonstructural facade and supporting columns are seen in a house based on works by this man, Villa Savoye. For 10 points, name this French author of the essay collection Towards a New Architecture including his "Five Points of Architecture".
items.a: Le Corbusier [or  Charles-Edouard Jeanneret , accept  Le Corb ]

items.q: The largest collection of buildings designed by this architect can be found in Detroit's Lafayette Park. Alexander Calder's Flamingo sculpture can be seen in front of the federal complex designed by this man in Chicago, where he also built high rise towers on Lake Shore Drive. This builder designed a namesake chair for his (*) Barcelona Pavilion and a mostly glass-walled retreat on stilts called the Farnsworth House. This man, the last director of the Bauhaus, collaborated with Philip Johnson on the Seagram Building. For 10 points, name this German architect whose building philosophy was that "less is more."
items.a: Ludwig Mies Van der Rohe [prompt on "Van der Rohe]

items.q: At a site originally occupied by Mecca Flats, this architect designed the Illinois Institute of Technology's Crown Hall. Another of this architect's works stands on 5-foot stilts and features white curtains along its glass walls. With Lilly Reich, this architect designed the iconic Brno chair while designing a three-story villa with a translucent onyx wall for Fritz and Grete (*) Tugendhat. This architect of the Farnsworth house designed apartment complexes on Lake Shore Drive. Non-structural I beams are found on the exterior of one building designed by this architect in collaboration with Philip Johnson, the Seagram Building. For 10 points, name this final director of the Bauhaus, a German architect who famously adopted maxims of "God is in the details" and "less is more."
items.a: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe [accept either underlined portion]

items.q: The only library designed by this architect was completed a few years after his 1969 death, and it was recently modernized to increase the amount of natural light. That library, located in northwest Washington, D.C., is this architect's Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library. For a 38-story building in midtown Manhattan, this architect designed most of the building, but two large restaurants inside it were designed by Philip Johnson. This designer of the Seagram Building was also the last director of the Bauhaus [rhymes with "cow house"]. For 10 points, name this German architect who often said "Less is more."
items.a: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe [prompt on van der Rohe]

items.q: This designer, who wrote that we should "create form out of the nature of our tasks with the methods of our time,"is often credited with the phrase "the devil is in the details." A credo of the industrial designer Dieter Rams adds the words "but better" to some of this designer's advice. This designer and a female collaborator created the Brno ("BUR-noh") chair while furnishing a villa for Fritz and Greta Tugendhat. This designer's frequent collaborator Lilly Reich worked with him to create an object with two rectangular leather surfaces for the 1929 International Exposition, the Barcelona chair. The Farnsworth House was designed by this last director of the Bauhaus ("BAO-house"). For 10 points, name this German architect of the International Style who co-designed the Seagram Building and coined the phrase "less is more."
items.a: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe [or Ludwig Mies van der Rohe]

items.q: This man designed the "Biggest Mirror Ever" in the form of the Bell Labs Holmdel Complex in New Jersey. This man created the headquarters of companies like John Deere, IBM, and the General Motors Technical Center. This man was known for his thin-shell concrete structures like the (*) Kresge Auditorium at MIT. This architect designed the main terminal of the Dulles airport and the TWA Flight Center, along with a stainless steel arch that is now the centerpiece of America's newest national park. For ten points, name this Finnish-American architect of the St. Louis Arch.
items.a: Eero Saarinen

items.q: One of this architect's buildings was used in the TV show Severance and was called the Bell Laboratories. Another of this architect's buildings was bombed during a rock concert, which caused cracks to form in its interior arch. This architect's Ingalls Rink is commonly nicknamed "the (*) Whale." This architect used an inverted catenary curve on a structure located on the banks of the Mississippi River. For 10 points, name this Finnish-American architect of the Gateway Arch.
items.a: Eero Saarinen [reject "Eliel Saarinen"]

items.q: 1. This architect added a cylindrical fireplace and the world's first conversation pit to the Miller House. This architect designed a concert hall with a green roof resembling one-eighth of a sphere. The bridge of the original USS Enterprise featured this architect's Tulip Chair. This architect of the (*) Kresge Auditorium at MᐧIᐧT and the TᐧWᐧA terminal at JᐧFᐧK airport designed a 630-foot-tall inverted catenary on the Mississippi River. For 10 points, name this Finnish architect of St. Louis' Gateway Arch.
items.a: Eero Saarinen [reject "Eliel Saarinen"]

items.q: The usage of tinted windows and black granite in this architect's only skyscraper led it to be nicknamed "Black Rock." Florence Knoll collaborated with this architect on a chair with angled armrests resembling a namesake insect and another which was featured on Star Trek. This architect's usage of thin concrete shells is exemplified by his design for (*) MIT's Kresge ("KRESS-ghee") Auditorium and a building whose roof resembles an airplane, theTWA Flight Center. This architect used a catenary curve as the basis for his most famous work. For 10 points, name the Finnish architect who designed St. Louis's Gateway Arch.
items.a: Eero Saarinen

items.q: This architect inlaid images of playing card suits into a traditional pavement path leading up to the Casino of Madeira in Funchal. While in exile, this architect designed a building with a massive underground "Worker's Hall" as a favor for the French Communist Party. This architect placed a blue glass annex now nicknamed his "Eye" atop a single yellow pillar in a design for his namesake museum. A residential building designed by this architect is currently under renovation, as the 72 million exterior tiles that make up its distinctive (*) S-shaped facade have begun to fall off. This artist designed a museum that features a winding red-carpeted ramp leading up to a white cupola, which is often noted to resemble a UFO. The Edificio Copan and Niteroi Contemporary Art Museum were designed by, for 10 points, what architect, who also designed most of his home country's capital of Brasilia?
items.a: Oscar Niemeyer [accept Oscar Ribeiro de Almeida Niemeyer Soares Filho] <MS>

items.q: One of this architect's buildings is the subject of the short story collection Ark Without Noah. A self-designed museum dedicated to this architect includes a wide eye-shaped tower balanced on a rectangular yellow tiled support. A belltower by this person widens towards the top and has two sides made of see-through lattices; Candido Portinari was responsible for a quasi-cubist mosaic on the main building of that building. This architect designed a building that is topped by two white domes, one facing down and one facing up; those domes symbolize the (*) bicameral legislature housed in that National Congress designed by this architect, which lies along an airplane-shaped city's Monumental Axis. A blue cathedral designed by this architect formed of several connecting arcs is dedicated to St. Francis of Assisi. For 10 points, name this creator of numerous hyperboloid arches who also helped design Brasilia.
items.a: Oscar Niemeyer

items.q: For one commission, this man designed a saucer-shaped art museum that is surrounded entirely by a reflecting pool. This architect used a sinuous facade design for another building, whose sand-colored wooden slats are visible from the outside. In addition to the Niteroi Contemporary Art Museum and the sprawling residential Copan Building, this architect designed a cathedral consisting of four concrete parabolas. That design by this architect was criticized for its outside murals, which mostly depicted its namesake, St. Francis of Assisi, and was part of this architect's (*) Pampulha Project. This architect is most associated with a city in which Juscelino Kubitschek asked him to design his country's National Congress and Supreme Federal Court. For 10 points, name this counterpart of Lucio Costa, an architect known for designing much of Brasilia.
items.a: Oscar Niemeyer

items.q: This architect designed a memorial including a "Hall of Acts" and a "Creativity Pavilion": the main portion of that memorial depicts a hand dripping blood in the shape of a map. A park designed by this man includes an Air Force Museum called "The Hut" and a white trapezoidal building with a red flame-like marquee over the entrance. This architect designed a church which the local bishop called "the devil's bomb shelter", which contains a tapestry copy of Picasso's Guernica. One of this man's most famous buildings is made of four concrete (*) parabolas and an inverted obelisk; this Church of St. Francis of Assisi was part of his Pampulha Project. His most famous large-scale project includes a hyperboloid cathedral made of 16 concrete columns. For 10 points, name this modern architect who designed most of Brasilia.
items.a: Oscar Niemeyer

items.q: Traditional Kanak huts inspired this architect's design for the Tjibaou Cultural Centre in New Caledonia. This architect preserved the oval test track of an old Fiat car factory for his renovation of Lingotto in Turin. Canaletto's paintings of spires inspired this architect's design for a skyscraper, whose nickname was derisively given when it was said to "tear through the heart of historic (*) London." The longest airport terminal in the world, over a mile long, was designed by this architect on an artificial island in Osaka Bay. Su and Richard Rogers collaborated with this architect for the "inside-out" exposed pipes of the Centre Pompidou. For 10 points, name this Italian architect behind Kansai International Airport and The Shard.
items.a: Renzo Piano

items.q: This architect drew inspiration from traditional Kanak Great Houses for the ten-pavilion Jean-Marie Tjibaou ("chee-BOW") Cultural Centre in Noumea. This architect called for Gozitan ("GO-zit-un") limestone slabs to be carved to appear eroded for the controversial zero-emission Parliament House of Malta. This architect replaced a Marcel Breuer-designed building in a Meatpacking District with a new terraced structure that opens to the High Line at the (*) Whitney Museum. A mile-long departure lounge is part of the world's longest airport terminal, which this architect designed on the artificial island of Kankujima. A glass-clad pyramidal skyscraper designed by this architect is the tallest building in the United Kingdom. For 10 points, name this Italian architect of Osaka's Kansai International Airport and The Shard.
items.a: Renzo Piano

items.q: The green roof of a museum redesigned by this architect in 2005 was inspired by the seven major hills of the city it's in. This architect of the California Academy of Sciences kept the brick facade of the Fogg Museum but added a glass pyramid roof in his renovation of the Harvard Art Museums' building. Like many of his other museums, the use of natural light is maximized in this architect's design for the modern wing of the Art Institute of (*) Chicago. This architect matched the industrial environment of the new location in his design for the Whitney Museum's new building. For 10 points name this architect who collaborated with Richard and Su Rogers on the Centre Pompidou.
items.a: Renzo Piano

items.q: This architect's glass-and-steel "Biosfera" is home to 150 species of flora and fauna and sits in Genoa's Porto Antico. This architect chose to leave the ruins of Edward Middleton Barry's Royal Opera House as an open-air space during the remodel of the Valletta City Gate. This man designed an entrance building to go with the McKim Building at the Morgan Library. This man's use of sliding joints helped a wing-shaped building survive the 1995 (*) Kobe earthquake unscathed despite its mile-long departure lounge. This man was the alphabetically-first designer of a museum that has its elevators, electrical wiring, and plumbing in colored tubes on the outside. For 10 points, what Italian architect designed the new Whitney Museum and collaborated with Richard Rogers on the Centre Pompidou?
items.a: Renzo Piano

items.q: An early work by this architect used stilts to hold cubes and prisms together for Cincinnati's Contemporary Arts Center. This architect used 26,000 fiberglass triangles for Zaragoza's Bridge Pavilion. This architect of Rome's MAXXI museum used a design based on the sails of Dhow boats for a soccer World Cup stadium. A design by this architect was analogized to (*) "two pebbles" being washed away on the Pearl River. This architect created a wave-shaped roof in the design of the London Aquatics Centre for the 2012 Olympics. For 10 points, the Guangzhou Opera House was designed by what British-Iraqi architect, the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize?
items.a: Zaha Hadid [or Dame Zaha Mohammad Hadid DBE RA]

items.q: This architect utilized the concept of a "Metonymic Landscape" in designing Seoul's Dongdaemun Design Plaza. Suspended black staircases contrast with the all-white interior of an art museum designed by this architect. Spectator wings were added to a venue designed by this architect for the 2012 London Olympics. A building designed by this architect resembles (*) two pebbles being washed away by the Pearl River. The Guangzhou Opera House and MAXXI Museum were designed by, for 10 points, what British-Iraqi female architect?
items.a: Zaha Hadid

items.q: A collaborator in this architect's firm used a term for self-generating systems to title the book The Autopoiesis of Architecture. This architect's graduation project was a plan for a Suprematist hotel on Hungerford Bridge called "Malevich's Tektonik." Patrik Schumacher coined a term often used to describe this architect's Dongdaemun (dong-DAY-mun) Design Plaza, "parametricism." This architect sued the New York Review of Books after being criticized for dismissing concerns over dying construction workers building the Al-Wakrah Stadium, which will be used for the 2022 World Cup. Two rocks being smoothed by the Pearl River inspired the flowing lines in the design of this architect's Guangzhou Opera House, which contributed to their nickname of the "queen of the curve." The MAXXI Museum was designed by, for 10 points, what Iraqi-British architect?
items.a: Zaha Hadid [Zaha Mohammad Hadid]

items.q: This architect used the concept of a "Metonymic Landscape" for Seoul's Dongdaemun Design Plaza. This architect's design for the Cardiff Bay Opera House lacked financial support and has never been realised, and plans for a bicycle helmet-shaped stadium in Meiji Park by this architect have also been scrapped. (*) This architect's completed projects include the BMW Central Building in Leipzig, and the "twin boulders" of Guangzhou Opera House. The designer of the London 2012 Aquatics Centre and the 2022 FIFA World Cup Stadium, for 10 points, name this Pritzker-winning female architect.
items.a: Zaha Hadid

items.q: This architect designed the scenery for a 1968 Billy Al Bengston exhibition at LACMA. This architect fixed a full-scale F-104 jet fighter to the entrance of the California Aerospace Museum. This architect's use of a fish motif appears in his design of a restaurant in Kobe. This architect's "open-ended" approach can be seen in the use of corrugated steel and mesh fencing of his Santa Monica residence. A building designed by this architect described as a "metaphoric city" has an atrium he nicknamed "the flower." This architect associated with Deconstructivism used concave wave-like exteriors for a Los Angeles concert hall. For 10 points, name this Canadian-American architect of the Walt Disney Concert Hall and Guggenheim Bilbao.
items.a: Frank Gehry [or Frank Owen Gehry; or Frank Owen Goldberg]

items.q: This architect and Gunter Pfiefer used white plaster and zinc alloy to create a continuous white swirl for the exterior of the Vitra Design Museum. This architect designed the "Flower" atrium for a building that revitalized a rundown port. This architect worked with Vlado Milunic on a building originally named Ginger and Fred. A building by this architect resembles a (*) ship along the Nevrion River wrapped in titanium scales. This architect utilized curved metallic sheets for the design for the Walt Disney Concert Hall. For 10 points, name this architect of the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao.
items.a: Frank Gehry [or Frank Owen Gehry or Frank Owen Goldberg] (The third clue references the Dancing House in Prague.)

items.q: This architect placed concrete columns that flank a tapestry of the Pointe du Hoc promontory in his Eisenhower Memorial. This architect and Vlado Milunic designed a rock tower and a glass tower for Prague's Dancing House. A smashed guitar inspired this architect's design for Seattle's Museum of Pop Culture. The Founders Room was sanded after its (*) reflectivity overheated sidewalks in a building designed by this architect. This architect pioneered digital design with his style of twisting metal sheets that grace a Spanish art museum. The Walt Disney Concert Hall was designed by, for 10 points, what architect who created the Guggenheim Bilbao?
items.a: Frank Gehry [or Frank Owen Gehry]

items.q: This architect collaborated with Claes Oldenburg to design the Chiat/Day Building, which features giant binoculars at its entrance. This architect added titled glass cubes to a home in Santa Monica. This designer of the Pritzker Pavilion was commissioned to create an extension of the Art Gallery of Ontario in his home city. To minimize reflection, this architect made modifications to the Founders Room of an LA concert hall dedicated to Walt Disney. This architect evoked a city's historic port on the Nervon river with a warped titanium-clad museum. For 10 points, name this deconstructivist architect of the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao.
items.a: Frank Gehry [or Frank Owen Gehry or Frank Owen Goldberg]

items.q: The first curtain wall to be designed by computer was in this architect's limestone- and marble-heavy design for the Morton H. Meyerson Symphony Center. This architect designed the Fountain Place skyscraper in that same city, where this architect added a redundant set of oval columns to a political office to assuage the mayor's fears that the 34-degree slope of its "inverted" walls was unstable. This architect used pink-tinted, bush-hammered concrete to emulate Anasazi cliff dwellings in his design for an NCAR facility. This architect of Dallas City Hall and Mesa Laboratory was taken on a road trip by Rolling Stone to brainstorm his "glass tent" design for a pyramid near Lake Erie. For 10 points, Cleveland's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame was designed by what Chinese-American architect?
items.a: I. M. Pei [or Ieoh Ming Pei]

items.q: This architect came out of retirement to design a building that was inspired by a light fountain from the Ibn Tulun Mosque. By hacking the window LED lights, students were able to play Tetris on this architect's Green Building at MIT. This architect connected a tetrahedral glass tent to a 162-foot-tall tower emerging from (*) Lake Erie for one building. Francois Mitterand commissioned this architect to design a glass-pane structure that serves as the main entrance to its namesake museum. For 10 points, name this Chinese-American architect of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and the Louvre Pyramid.
items.a: I. M. Pei [or Ieoh Ming Pei] (First line clues the Museum of Islamic Art in Doha.)

items.q: This architect was partly awarded the commission for one building because they were born the same year as the person the building is named for. This architect was inspired by Anasazi (ah-nuh-SAA-zee) cliff dwellings for the headquarters of the National Center for Atmospheric Research, the Mesa Laboratory in Boulder, Colorado. This designer of the (*) JᐧFᐧK Presidential Library designed a large atrium for a part of a building that they split into two triangles, the National Gallery of Art's East Building. This architect designed an all-glass structure with 673 panes outside of a museum. For 10 points, name this Chinese-American architect of the Rock n' Roll Hall of Fame and the pyramid at the Louvre.
items.a: I. M. Pei [or Ieoh Ming Pei]

items.q: One design by this architect consists of a rhombus-shaped pedestal and a lopsided conical dome that includes a large atrium. Myriad Convention Center and Myriad Botanical Gardens were projects created under this man's namesake redevelopment plan for Oklahoma City. This architect of the Macau Science Center designed the Pueblo-inspired (*) Mesa Laboratory in Boulder, Colorado as well as another design in Doha, Qatar inspired by the Ahmad Ibn Tulun Mosque. That building is the Museum of Islamic Art. Asymmetrical triangular frames resembling the growth patterns of bamboo can be found in this architect's 72-story Bank of China Tower. For 10 points, name this Chinese-American architect of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as well as the Louvre's glass pyramid.
items.a: I.M. Pei [or Ieoh Ming Pei; accept Pei plan]

items.q: As a professor at Southern Illinois University, this architect collaborated with John McHale on the inauguration of the World Design Science Decade in 1965, during which he led the field of "synergetics." Inspired by the sight of metal grain silos, this architect designed many circular steel shelters for World War II soldiers. This architect designed the American pavilion for the 1967 Montreal Expo, though it is now an environmental museum after it was damaged in a fire. A three-wheeled vehicle and an aluminum house designed by this architect are both described with the word "Dymaxion." This architect coined the term "Spaceship Earth," and his style is emulated in a structure in Disney World's Epcot Park. For 10 points, name this American architect who designed many geodesic domes.
items.a: Buckminster Fuller [or Richard Buckminster Fuller]

items.q: This man envisioned a giant umbrella covering a massive crater for Old Man River City, his proposal for a new East St. Louis. With Shoji Sadao and John McHale, this man designed a structure where visitors to an exhibition could play the World Game. A proto-form of a vertical indoor farm was included in designs for this man's (+) Growth Home of 1952. One house designed by this man featured a revolving closet called the "O-volving shelf" and had a "fog gun" rather than a conventional shower or bath. This man partnered with Wichita's Beech Aircraft to build two prototype postwar homes, one of which was bought in 2011 by the (*) Henry Ford Museum. Those homes designed by this man have a shape often compared to a Hershey's Kiss. This architect designed the Geoscope for the US Pavilion at Expo 67. For 10 points, name this creator of the Dymaxion House and stan for geodesic domes.
items.a: Buckminster Fuller

items.q: A group called CHARAS received a loan from New York City to create public housing in the fashion of this architect. Henry Kaiser funded a prototype of this man's three-wheeled car that could do easy 180-degree turns. He designed an factory-made, airplane-delivered "Dwelling Machine" that failed to catch on. His signature type of building embodied his mantra of "doing more with less" by using interlocking (*) triangles to provide strength. Many of his projects were given names including the term "Dymaxion." This architect's "Spaceship Earth" idea was incorporated in Disney's Epcot park, and he designed a similar spherical structure for the US Pavilion at the 1967 Montreal Expo. He lends his name to a 60-carbon allotrope. For 10 points, name this American architect who promoted the geodesic dome.
items.a: Buckminster Fuller [or Richard Buckminster Fuller]

items.q: This man's epitaph "Call me Trim Tab" is derived from an interview he gave to Playboy in 1972. He's not Adlai Stevenson, but this man popularised the term "Spaceship Earth", and was the second World President of Mensa. Signalling a commitment to the principles of rationality and efficiency in construction, a house, a map, and a car, among other things designed by this man, are prefaced by the word (*) "Dymaxion" . He was associated with, and lived in, a hemispherical structure designed to be easy to assemble quickly. For 10 points, name this American architect and designer, after whom an allotrope of carbon is named.
items.a: Buckminster Fuller

items.q: This artist created a generative artwork named after the "seedlings" of a Ghost Forest in Madison Square. One of this artist's "earth drawings," Wave Field, is on the University of Michigan's campus. This artist inscribed years in a spiral pattern on a granite table on Yale's campus. Frederick Hart's (*) Three Soldiers statue was placed next to a V-shaped installation by this artist composed of two black granite walls engraved with the names of soldiers. For 10 points, name this architect who designed the Vietnam Veterans War Memorial.
items.a: Maya Lin [or Maya Ying Lin]

items.q: In 2021, this architect installed 49 dead cedar trees in Madison Square Park in Ghost Forest, an installation that is part of this architect's What Is Missing? project. A sculpture of nurses by Glenna Goodacre was built as a "Women's" counterpart to a design by this architect. This architect was inspired by the Serpent Mounds to create "earth drawings" such as The Wave Field. This architect imagined "taking a knife and cutting into the earth" for a project that beat Frederick Hart's design in a 1981 competition. While an undergraduate at Yale, this architect designed two black granite walls where visitors rub the inscribed names of deceased soldiers onto paper. For 10 points, name this architect who designed Washington DC's Vietnam Veterans Memorial.
items.a: Maya Lin

items.q: This architect replanted forty-nine dead white cedars in Madison Square Park for a project called Ghost Forest. This architect designed a circle of stones called the Peace Chapel for Juniata College, where they delivered a convocation speech calling the work of an artist "a strong, clear vision." Johnpaul Jones collaborated with this architect on a series of installations along the Columbia and Snake Rivers in the (*) Confluence Project. This architect created undulating patterns of knolls in Ann Arbor, Michigan as the first of three Wave Fields. A site designed by this architect was supplemented with Frederick Hart's The Three Soldiers in 1984; that site designed by this architect is composed of two black granite walls in the shape of a "V." For 10 points, name this Chinese-American architect of the Vietnam Veterans' Memorial.
items.a: Maya (Ying) Lin

items.q: The Haley Farm in Clinton, Tennessee is the site of a library designed by this artist dedicated to Langston Hughes. This artist created a series of seven earthworks chronicling exchanges between European settlers and indigenous peoples along the Columbia River in the Confluence Project. In another work by this artist, a Martin Luther King quote is engraved onto a wall behind a memorial table that documents historic advances in civil rights. The names of female students at (*) Yale University are engraved onto a slab of black granite in this artist's Women's Table. Her most famous work is located near The Three Soldiers monument in Washington D.C. and descends gradually on a gradient; that work lists the names of 58,000 deceased soldiers along two granite walls that form a "V." For 10 points, name this Chinese-American architect of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial.
items.a: Maya Lin

items.q: This musician played the opening solo on Gil Evans's arrangement of "St. Louis Blues" for New Bottle Old Wine. One of his albums features the first recording of the Miles Davis composition "Nardis." On the first side of one of his albums, he paired his popular version of Cole Porter's "Love for Sale" with "Autumn Leaves," which also titles a 1963 live album of his that emerged from the same Japanese tour as Nippon Soul. This musician referred to Bobby Timmons's "This Here" as "Dis Here," and performed it along with "Dat Dere." He recorded the album Somethin' Else. His namesake quintet recorded a popular version of "Work Song," by his cornetist brother Nat. For 10 points, name this nickname-sporting jazz saxophonist who had a hit with "Mercy, Mercy, Mercy."
items.a: Cannonball Adderley [or Julian Edwin Adderley]

items.q: A 2022 NPR essay by Lara Downes describes [read slowly] "1-2, 1-5, 1-5, 1-5" fingerings often used to play this piece. This piece modulates to F Major for its "Trio" section before a reprise of its intro and then returning to C Major. This piano piece opens with both hands repeating the phrase [read slowly] "D, E, C, A [pause] B, G." John Stark first published this piece that was designed to be played (*) "not fast." The popularity of this piece was largely revived by Marvin Hamlisch's 1973 adaptation of it for the film The Sting. This "two step" piece, often used by ice cream vans, was named in honor of "James Brown and his Mandolin Club." For 10 points, name this Scott Joplin ragtime piece named for a profession.
items.a: "The Entertainer"

items.q: To decorate these structures, architects used muqarnas that originally developed from supportive squinches. A major pendentive type of these structures exists in a building designed by Isidorus of Miletus. A sacred building named for a gold-covered one of these structures is located on (*) Temple Mount in Jerusalem. One of these structures designed by Brunelleschi sits atop Florence's Cathedral. The roof of St. Basil's Cathedral in Moscow is decorated with numerous colorful structures of this type. For 10 points, name these architectural structures commonly found on the roofs of mosques.
items.a: domes

items.q: New York resident Kevin Shea lives in one of these structures, dubbed the Long Island Green one of these structures. Norman Foster designed a glass one of these structures to symbolize the reunification of Germany for the Reichstag. The largest brick one of these structures in the world was designed by Filippo (*) Brunelleschi and adorns the top of the Florence Cathedral. For 10 points, name this architectural feature that can be found predominantly atop the U.S. Capital, and is loosely defined as the top half of a sphere.
items.a: domes [or sphere; or geodesic sphere before "Foster" is read]

items.q: The royal chapel at the church of Les Invalides features one of these designed by Jules Mansart. In Islamic architecture, muqarnas often decorate these structures and the squinches supporting them. The Mycenaeans constructed the Treasury of Atreus as a corbled one of these. Another of these structures is supported by four buttressed pendentives in the Hagia Sophia, and the one at Florence Cathedral is topped with a cupola and was designed by Brunelleschi. Coffers and an oculus help reduce the weight of this structure at the Pantheon in Rome. For 10 points, name these architectural elements, one of which sits prominently atop the U.S. Capitol.
items.a: domes

items.q: An octagonal brick version of this structure was engineered for the Santa Maria del Fiore by Brunelleschi, and a famous Roman one features an Oculus. Four pendentives support this structure in Istanbul's Hagia Sophia, and nine of these structures sit atop a prominent cathedral in Moscow. For 10 points, name this architectural feature seen atop the Pantheon and the Taj Mahal, which occurs on St. Basil's Cathedral in an "onion" shape.
items.a: Domes

items.q: A small one of these objects sits atop an elephant in a sculpture in the Piazza della Minerva that inspired figures in several Dali paintings. One of these objects was installed by Domenico Fontana 100 years before an architect surrounded it with extended, curving colonnades in a design for a square. One of these objects that is topped by a Pamphili emblem stands in the (*) Piazza Navona. That object sits above gods representing the Nile, Ganges, Danube, and Rio de la Plata in the Fountain of the Four Rivers by Bernini. Along with columns, many of these tall structures were brought to Rome from temples in Heliopolis and Karnak. For 10 points, name these ancient Egyptian stone towers whose modern day equivalents include the Washington Monument.
items.a: obelisks [prompt on fountains by asking "what kind of object is included in the fountain design?"]

items.q: Sir William Chambers designed one of these buildings in London's Kew Gardens that unusually contains an even number of floors. A single swaying wooden pillar was used to build many traditional types of these buildings. These buildings inspired the design of the world's tallest LEED-certified building, which is decorated with swirling ruyi motifs. An octagonal brick one of these buildings from the Song Dynasty is nicknamed for resembling (*) rusted iron, while two are named for Wild Geese in Xi'an. Taipei 101's design was inspired by these buildings, which evolved from the related stupa. For 10 points, name these multi-tiered towers with many eaves that are common across Asian countries.
items.a: pagodas [or ta; accept Great Wild Goose Pagoda; accept Small Wild Goose Pagoda; prompt on Buddhist temples by asking "what type of building were these temples?"]

items.q: A small one of these structures built atop a precariously perched rock covered in gold leaf is nicknamed the Golden Rock. One of these structures was the largest in a "royal circuit" of architectural styles that William Chambers built for Princess Augusta. In one country, these structures are topped by a hti("tee"), which is an umbrella topped with precious stones. Two lion sculptures called Chinthe("cheen-theh") flank the entrance to a structure of this type for which the Great (*) Bell of Dhammazedi was constructed. An octagonal one of these structures was nicknamed due to its glazed bricks' resemblance to iron. Two merchants supposedly chose the site for a massive golden one of these structures which houses eight strands of the Buddha's hair. For 10 points, Yangon's Shwedagon is an example of what Buddhist tiered towers?
items.a: pagodas [or ta; accept stupa; prompt on temples]

items.q: One of these structures designed by Danish architect Johann Otto von Spreckelsen is slightly tilted to accommodate the metro and rail stations below it. Copies of the horses at St. Mark's Basilica in Venice stand atop one of these structures in the Place du Carrousel. A third one of these structures stands in the middle of a "Square of the Star" where twelve avenues converge. A "grande" one of these structures in the La Defense district was opened on Bastille Day 1989 and was part of Francois Mitterrand's "Grand Projects." John Nash designed one of these structures in London named for its marble construction. A tomb of the unknown soldier lies under one of these structures that was built after the Battle of Austerlitz and based on one commissioned by Titus. For 10 points, name this kind of structure exemplified by a Neoclassical one "of Triumph" in Paris that celebrates Napoleon's victories.
items.a: triumphal arch [accept Arc de Triomphe; accept Grande Arche]

items.q: Literally meaning "cooking-pot," this term was coined by German geologist Leopold von Buch to describe features associated with ring dykes, such as the ones at Yellowstone and Krakatoa. These (*) volcanic features are generally formed as a result of explosive eruptions, in which the rapid emptying of the magma chamber causes the volcano to collapse inward. For 10 points, identify this cauldron-like volcanic feature, often confused with a crater.
items.a: Caldera

items.q: These structural features are sometimes classified into two groups dependent on the presence of a strong positive or negative gravity anomaly. The second of these includes those that form from slow, stepwise subsidence, or the Masayan type, and those in which a vacuum is created by migration to adjacent chambers, the Atitlan type. All of the largest ones fall under the Valles classification, in which intrusion along arcuate faults creates a characteristic circular structure sometimes exposed by their erosion. That pattern, known as a ring dike, is typically offset by a concentric normal fault system, as rock slides inward to accommodate a sudden loss of supporting material. For 10 points, name this kind of depression resulting from the collapse of a volcano.
items.a: caldera

items.q: A glacial type of these features that coincides with ice-contact ridges is often named for forming atop kames. Crossbedding can be seen in these features' foreset or front, which are older than a "pro" prefixed part of them. These features may be analogized to a bird's foot due to their lobes, whose avulsion causes these features' namesake "switching." Outward progradation of these features' namesake plains contributes to the formation of mouth bars. These features are rare in low endorheic basins, where alluvial fans form instead. These features' many distributaries are widened and deepened by tides. For 10 points, name these triangular plains of sediment typically found where rivers drain.
items.a: deltas [or delta plains; prompt on river mouths until "mouth bars" is read]

items.q: An operator denoted by this single letter can be defined as the trace of the Hessian matrix. On the torus, the Dirichlet kernel can be used to approximate a function denoted by this letter which equals the derivative of the Heaviside step function. A discrete function named for this letter gives one if both its inputs are equal and zero otherwise, and is named after Leopold (*) Kronecker. Both the modular discriminant and the Laplacian are denoted by the capital of this letter. Along with epsilon, this Greek letter often denotes small changes. When calculating the slope of a line, this Greek letter often prepends x and y to denote differences. For 10 points, name this fourth letter of the Greek alphabet.
items.a: delta [accept Dirac delta function or Kronecker delta function; prompt on del squared before "Dirichlet"]

items.q: A 5-4-isomerase named for this letter is the dehydrogenase ("de-hy-DRODG-en-ase") which produces the ketone on testosterone and converts between classes of steroid named for this letter. The input to the porphyrin synthesis pathway has a name that begins with this Greek letter because it is a five-carbon amino acid with no sidechains. A numerical superscript on this letter is used to indicate where there's a gap in the double bonds of a cyclic molecule, which differentiates isomers of (*) THC. Covalent bonds named for this letter have two lobal planes and thus four distinct lobes. The lineage B.1.617.2 is named for this letter and is a more transmissible variant of COVID-19 capable of reinfecting vaccinated individuals. For 10 points, bonds between d orbitals are named for what fourth Greek letter?
items.a: delta [accept delta-aminolevulinic acid, delta-8-THC, delta-9-THC, ; prompt on A or d before "Greek" with "what Greek letter?"]

items.q: A company with this name investigated Senator Roger Wicker after he was spotted with his mask down to his chin. The hashtag #EndSARS trended on social media after a video of a cop shooting a motorist in a Nigerian state with this name went viral. A hurricane with this name left Louisiana buildings without power 6 weeks after Hurricane Laura. An (*) airline with this name led by CEO Ed Bastian announced in 2020 that it would retire its fleet of Boeing 777s. A 2020 hurricane in the American Southwest and the second largest airline in the world were both named after, for 10 points, what Greek letter with a triangle shape?
items.a: delta [accept Delta Airlines or Delta State or Hurricane Delta ]

items.q: A valley named for these things on the Kamchatka Peninsula was partially destroyed by a 2007 mudslide. A nonprofit that tracks these things offers rebuild stats for American examples such as Daisy and Beehive. A "cold" one of these things in Germany called the Brubbel is unusually powered by carbon dioxide. The English word for these things comes from a "Great" one in (*) Iceland located near another one called Strokkur. One of these things known as Steamboat was dormant from 1968 to 1978 but has a higher peak than a nearby cone example that has a consistent interval of 44 minutes. For 10 points, name these natural features exemplified by Yellowstone's Old Faithful.
items.a: geysers [accept cold-water geyser]

items.q: These geologic entities come in fountain and cone varieties. Two of these named "Vent" and "Turban" help predict the activity of one of these named "Grand." They are caused near fissures and cavities in the rock when magma near the Earth's surface (*) heats a source of water. Mostly found in the Western United States and Iceland, for 10 points, name this type of violently erupting hot spring, such as Yellowstone's Old Faithful.
items.a: geyser (prompt on "(hot) spring")

items.q: The Sif-Gula region of Venus forms complexes of these structures, where these objects do not observe the linear patterning they do on Earth. The lava that forms them tends to form rocks without gas bubbles, and when they erupt, frequently a fissure along their sides will form, creating spatter ramparts in a phenomenon called a curtain of fire, though on the whole their eruptions are characterized as relatively calm. For 10 points, identify these volcanoes formed by low-viscosity basaltic lava, exemplified by Mauna Loa and Mauna Kea, best known for their broad, shallow sides.
items.a: shield volcano [prompt on volcano]

items.q: Moderator Note: Read answerline fully The Hudson Canyon lies in one of these things, which are often covered by relict sediments from the Ice Age. One of these named Campeche is an exception to the trend that active margins have smaller examples of them. Doggerland is on one of these things, while the Sunda one ends at Wallace's Line. These entities are made of neritic and (*) benthic zones. These regions end at namesake "breaks," after which there is a steeper "slope," and they are often exposed with lower sea levels. For 10 points, name these submerged extensions of continent, the shallowest parts of the seabed.
items.a: continental shelf [accept bank; prompt on general descriptions of the seafloor; do not accept or prompt on any other specific parts of the bottom of the sea]

items.q: This artist's lover Tommaso dei Cavalieri modeled for The Genius of Victory, a sculpture intended to stand with unfinished statues of figures partially titled "Atlas" and "Awakening." The Galleria dell'Accademia contains a statue by this artist whose disproportionate head and right hand were intended for its viewing at the top of the Florence Cathedral. Statues of a Dying Slave, Rebellious Slave, and a Horned Moses were created by this artist for the tomb of Pope Julius II. This artist, who only signed his 1499 version of the Pieta, created a 17-foot tall statue that looks into the distance and holds a sling over his shoulder. For 10 points, name this Renaissance artist of a marble David.
items.a: Michelangelo [or Michelangelo Buonarroti or Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni]

items.q: This artist may have included a self-portrait as Nicodemus in his final sculpture of the Deposition. This artist gave drawings of Zeus and Ganymede to his gay lover, Tommaso dei Cavalieri. Daniele da Volterra earned the nickname "the Breeches Maker" for altering this artist's paintings. This artist's likeness inspired a pensive Heraclitus at the bottom of (*) Raphael's School of Athens. This artist depicted himself as St. Bartholomew's flayed skin in a scene of the Last Judgment. For a commission by Pope Julius II, this artist used custom scaffolding to paint scenes from Genesis such as one in which two fingers nearly touch. For 10 points, The Creation of Adam was painted by what artist on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
items.a: Michelangelo [or Michelangelo Buonarroti; prompt on Buonarroti] (Daniele de Volterra was commissioned by Pope Paul VI to cover up some of Michelangelo's nudes in the Sistine Chapel.)

items.q: Four fingers of a sculpture by this artist were mended by Giuseppe Lirioni after they were broken during relocation; that sculpture is the only work by this artist to feature their signature. One fresco by this artist features twenty seated male nudes called ignudi. This artist commissioned the sculptures Dying Slave andRebellious Slave for the tomb of Pope (*) Julius II. The titular figure lies on a green hill and reaches to grab God's extended finger in this artist's The Creation of Adam.
