A 17 foot marble statue by this artist is unusually depicted without the head of Goliath. For 10 points, name this sculptor of a marble David and painter of the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
items.a: Michelangelo [or Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni]

items.q: This artist created Rebellious Slave and Dying Slave for the tomb of Pope Julius II, and signed the sash of a sculpture in which a youthful Mary holds the body of Jesus. A contrapposto nude sculpture holding a slingshot and The (*) Creation of Adam are works by this sculptor of the Piet`a. For 10 points, name this Italian Renaissance artist who sculpted a marble David and painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.
items.a: Michelangelo (accept Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni)

items.q: A painting in this artistic period depicts the crucified Christ with plague-like sores. That painting, the Isenheim [EE-zen-hime] Altarpiece, was a notable triptych [TRIP-tik] of this artistic period. Another painting from this artistic period depicts an (*) anamorphic skull at the feet of two titular figures and is titled The Ambassadors. Hans Holbein was active during a "Northern" artistic period with this name. For 10 points, name this artistic period that integrated religious tradition with everyday life and led to a "rebirth" of art.
items.a: Renaissance [accept Northern Renaissance; accept German Renaissance; accept Swiss Renaissance]

items.q: One movement with this name involved painters like Aaron Douglas and Jacob Lawrence, who were influenced by African folk art. In addition to that "Harlem" movement, another period by this name flourished in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries and was based on humanism and classical influences. Raphael and Leonardo da Vinci were part of, for 10 points, what period of art whose name is French for "rebirth"?
items.a: Renaissance [accept "Harlem Renaissance" until "Harlem"; accept variants such as "Early Renaissance" or "High Renaissance"]

items.q: One artist from this movement included his Modern Magic series among many African-inspired handcrafted quilts, sculptures, and paintings for his first solo exhibition, Restitution of the Mind and Soul. That artist from this movement created a colorful bookcase of American "activists," and suspended a shoe made of Dutch wax with an invisible wire in two other works. Years after building the house of another artist from this movement, David Adjaye built a walnut-paneled room for an installation of 13 paintings by that artist depicting (*) rhesus macaque monkeys. Another artist from this movement created a large model of Nelson's Ship in a Bottle for the Fourth Plinth of Trafalgar Square, while a more famous work by him depicts a woman wearing fake Chanel fabric in a headless version of The Swing that used Ankara fabric. An artist from this movement who created The Upper Room and No Woman No Cry was attacked by Rudy Giuliani for using elephant dung in a depiction of a Black Madonna. For 10 points, name this art movement whose members include Yinka Shonibare and Chris Ofili, the latter of whom feuded with Stuckists following a scandal involving the Tate Gallery.
items.a: Young British Artists [or YBA; accept Brit artists]

items.q: One member of this art movement painted two stacked red circles on a pink background in his work Snowman. Another member of this movement had a work where ten blue-overalled workers and large grinding machines destroyed every one of his possessions in a pseudo-assembly line process. In addition to Gary Hume and Michael Landy, this art movement had an artist with a work that contained close-ups of female genitalia collaged with (*) elephant dung in his The Holy Virgin Mary, which famously offended Rudy Guiliani. Another work from this movement was jumped on by the performance artists Yuan Chai and Jian Jun X and contained bloody underwear and used condoms. For 10 points, name this art movement whose notable works include Tracy Emin's My Bed and Damien Hirst's The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living.
items.a: Young British Artists [or YBA; prompt on Britart; prompt on Brit artists; prompt on Young Brits]

items.q: One of its first shows included a work where a shot to the head was blown up over an interlocking grid of fifteen separate framed images, Mat Collishaw's Bullet Hole; that student-run show was Freeze. Bullet Hole was purchased by a man who is acknowledged to be one of its main sponsors, art collector and advertiser Charles Saatchi. After a May 2004 fire, Saatchi's collection lost a work, a blue tent that bore several appliqued names inside, entitled Everyone I Have Ever Slept With 1963-1995 by Royal Academy member Tracey Emin. One of its members produced a work whose original incarnation decayed; that work is a vitrine holding a tiger shark preserved in formaldehyde and is Damien Hirst's The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living. For 10 points, name this group of artists who in 1988 started to exhibit together in London.
items.a: Young British Artists or Brit artists or Britart

items.q: A nude Andromeda on the left with her back to the viewer watches an armor-clad Perseus perform the title action in his Perseus Slaying the Sea Monster. He was also fond of painting series as in his The Heart Desires and The Soul Attains, two parts of his Pygmalion and Galatea cycle, and his large four-part group about Sleeping Beauty, the Briar Rose paintings. A male nude in his Phyllis and Demophoon caused scandal but the three male nudes in his canvas Wheel of Fortune resulted in little outcry. His artistic diversity is reflected in the numerous stained glass windows and book illustrations, such as those for an 1896 edition of Chaucer, which he did for the workshop of his friend William Morris. An abiding interest in Arthurian myth, typified by his painting The Beguiling of Merlin, also characterized, for 10 points, what Pre-Raphaelite artist and painter of King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid?
items.a: Edward Coley Burne-Jones

items.q: This sculpture replaced a temporary one incorporating the quote "To my words they durst add nothing, and my speech dropped upon them" from the Book of Job. Many were surprised when Charles Ricketts was passed over for this sculpture's commission by Robert Ross, especially because the chosen artist's only previous commission was a controversial set of nudes for the headquarters of the British Medical Association. Aleister Crowley placed a (*) butterfly-shaped plaque on this sculpture, which was soon removed because it infuriated the artist. Assyrian figures at the British Museum may have inspired this sculpture's figure of a sphinx in flight, whose rather large testicles were removed by vandals in 1961. It is now surrounded by a glass barrier because so many people would put lipstick on and then kiss it. For 10 points, name this Jacob Epstein sculpture in Pere Lachaise cemetery which memorializes an Irish author.
items.a: the tomb of Oscar Wilde

items.q: One of these religious structures has a "Cannibal Hymn" inscribed on its walls as part of a "Text" named for these places, and was built for Teti. One of these structures near Saqqara was built for Djoser [JOH-sur] by Imhotep. (*) Mastabas were a "stepped" type of these structures, three of which were built for rulers like Khafre and Khufu near Giza. For 10 points, name this large, imposing kind of structure where Egyptian pharaohs were buried.
items.a: pyramids (accept pyramids of Giza; accept descriptions of specific pyramids, such as the Pyramid of Teti, Djoser, Menkaure, Khafre, and/or Khufu; prompt on more general terms like "tomb," "necropolis," or "burial place")

items.q: One of these religious structures at Abu Rawash was built for Dje-defre and destroyed by the Romans. In these structures, serdabs held Ka statues that could receive the smell of offerings. One of these structures in Saqqara, designed by Imhotep for (*) Djoser, adapted the older mastaba into a "stepped" one of these structures. Three of these structures built for Menkaure, Khafre, and Khufu dominate a necropolis near Giza. For 10 points, name this kind of structure used to bury pharaohs in ancient Egypt.
items.a: pyramids (accept pyramids of Giza; accept Pyramid of Djedefre, Djoser, Menkaure, Khafre, and/or Khufu; prompt on more general terms like "tomb," "necropolis," or "burial place")

items.q: The tallest skyscraper in San Francisco is known as the "Transamerica" this due to its distinctive shape. One urban legend regarding one structure of this type says that it has 666 glass panes. A banner reading "Novus Ordo Seclorum" in one artwork is located underneath one structure of this type, which is topped by the (*) Eye of Providence. Two ziggurats in Luxor Las Vegas surround one structure of this type, a "step" one of which was also built at Chichen Itza. For 10 points, name these triangular structures that contain tombs of pharaohs, including some "Great" ones in Giza.
items.a: pyramids

items.q: Many of these structures were built by the Igbo people in Nsude to worship the earth deity Ala. Kushite kings often built these structures in large settlements like Meroe. One of these structures can be found in Teotihuacan along the Avenue of the (*) Dead and was named after the sun by the later Aztecs. The only remaining of the Seven Ancient Wonders of the World is one of these structures, which was built by Fourth Dynasty Pharaoh Khufu. For 10 points, name these structures which in Egyptian culture served as burial monuments holding mummified remains.
items.a: Pyramids [accept more specific answer like Step Pyramids] <Peter>

items.q: Norman Mailer's last novel, which recounts a demon's visit to the young Adolf Hitler, is titled for one of these structures "in the forest." A novel partly named for this kind of structure portrays the poisoning of four members of the Blackwood family, a crime for which Constance is blamed though the culprit is her sister Merricat. That novel is titled We Have Always Lived in [one of these buildings]. In another novel titled for this kind of structure Conrad is crushed by a giant helmet; that novel is titled for one of these buildings of Otranto. For 10 points, in a Franz Kafka novel, K. tries and fails to gain entrance into what kind of royal residence?
items.a: castles

items.q: The trace italienne was an improvement on these buildings and replaced the enceinte version, which contained "dead zones" created by curved structures. The comte de Vauban ("comb de vo-BAHN") developed his "third system," or "perfected Landau system," as a designer of these places, like one at Strasbourg. The Bailey, an enclosed courtyard, was a component of an early version of this kind of structure. Mont Saint-Michel ("moan sant mi-SHELL") and Neuschwanstein ("NOYSH-von-styne") are current popular ones. The Windsor one is located in the United Kingdom. These buildings often had battlements from which archers could fire, as well as moats. For 10 points, name these buildings that fortified medieval Europe.
items.a: castles [accept fortifications until mention; accept chateaus; do not accept or prompt on "palaces"] <CL>

items.q: William Pereira primarily used glass and this material to design the Geisel Library at UCSD. A key element of Tadao Ando's work involves cutting holes in this material, such as a cross for his Church of the Light in Osaka. Israeli architect (*) Moshe Safdie primarily used this material to design his Habitat 67 apartment complex. For many of his modernist buildings, Le Corbusier utilized an unfinished form of this material called "Beton brut." For 10 points, name this material which is often used in a "reinforced" form for Brutalist designs.
items.a: reinforced concrete [accept reinforced cement concrete or Portland cement concrete or ready-mixed concrete; accept beton brut; reject "cement"]

items.q: A narrow water channel bisects a plaza around which two symmetrical buildings made of this material frame a view of the Pacific Ocean at Louis Kahn's Salk Institute. A housing complex designed for Montreal's Expo 67 consists of 354 connected components made of this material. A cross cut into a wall made of this material is illuminated during the day in Tadao Ando's Church of the (*) Light. Le Corbusier ("luh cor-booz-yay") used this material for Chandigarh's ("chun-di-gar's") Palace of Assembly and High Court of Justice, where, like many of his other modernist designs, this material is left exposed and unfinished. For 10 points, Brutalist architecture makes heavy use of what construction material, composed of aggregate and cement?
items.a: reinforced concrete [accept reinforced cement concrete, accept Portland cement concrete, accept ready-mixed concrete, accept beton brut, do not accept or prompt on just "cement"]

items.q: Barnabas Calder's book on this material celebrates Denys Lasdun's use of it. A "king" of this material uses blue plastic cones to create his trademark holes within it, and used it for the Church of the Light in Osaka. The taxidermist Carl Akeley made a "gun" used to spray this material, which was used to create the "gunnite" sections of a building whose irregularly-placed windows produce a speckled effect on the wall behind the (*) altar. An unfinished form of this material was used in Marseille's Unite d'Habitation ("oo-nee-TAY dah-bee-tah-SYOHN") and is referred to by the French term "Beton brut" ("BAY-ton broo"). Thick walls of this material support the curved roof of the Notre Dame du Haut ("NOH-truh DAHM doo OWE"). For 10 points, name this material used in many Modernist buildings of Le Corbusier, and which can be "reinforced" with steel.
items.a: reinforced concrete [accept reinforced cement concrete or Portland cement concrete or ready-mixed concrete; do not accept or prompt on just "cement"]

items.q: Four photos of grid-like arrangements in this material were composited to make an early work by a female sculptor, titled [This material] Visions. Four tubes of this material were arranged to make a cross shape in the middle of nowhere, Utah, by Nancy Holt. The artistic use of this material was pioneered by Auguste Perret. Denys Lasdun's extensive use of this material was attacked by Nikolaus Pevsner, who savaged Paul (*) Rudolph's use of it in a "dedicatory" speech for one of Rudolph's works. "Paulistas" like Paulo Mendes da Rocha emphasize the use of this material. This material was hammered at to create a "pitted" surface at the Barbican. This was the primary material used in the paired-tower designs of Erno Goldfinger. This material was used, undecorated, for the roof of Notre Dame du Haut, and it's the main material used in the Marseille Cite radieuse. For 10 points, name this building material whose "raw" form gives the name to Brutalist architecture.
items.a: reinforced concrete [accept beton brut; accept Concrete Visions]

items.q: One structure in this style contains a fresco of Prince Vijaya amidst a row of elephants carrying men who hold parasols. A group of structures built in this form contains a fresco of a dark figure with a peaked crown who looks down while holding a lotus blossom, the so-called "Beautiful Bodhisattva." Another building in this form has two levels of columns and pediments, with the split halves of the upper pediment separated by a central crowned pillar. A complex in this architectural form built under Gebre Mesqel is split in half by a river and arranged to mirror the Holy Land's geography. Bete Giyorgis, or the Church of St. George, is a work of this type that sits in a hole in the ground and is shaped like a (*) cross. This type of architecture was used for many churches in Ethiopia's holy city of Lalibela, and also for structures in the hills of Cappadocia. For 10 points, name this architectural form exemplified by the Treasury in Petra, which was hewn out of the side of a sandstone wall.
items.a: rock-cut architecture [accept caves before "two levels"] [3]

items.q: Anna Chave claimed this style represented "the face of capital, the face of authority" in an essay about its "rhetoric of power." Artists of this movement are critiqued as overly theatrical "literalists" in Michael Fried's "Art and Objecthood." An artist from this movement called illusionism "one of the salient and most objectionable relics of European art" in the essay "Specific Objects." Speaking about one of his works, an artist of this movement remarked "Six feet has a suggestion of being cooked. Six foot box. Six foot under." Robert Pincus-Witten described the work of Eva Hesse as "post-[this movement]." An artist who worked in this style used materials like galvanized (*) iron and plexiglass for identical units evenly spaced up a wall in a series of untitled pieces. This style is exemplified by a 6-by-6-by-6 steel cube titled Die by Tony Smith and the boxes of Donald Judd. For 10 points, name this sculptural style characterized by extreme simplicity of form.
items.a: minimalism [or minimal art]

items.q: A character originally from this film urges "Don't turn away from love" in an homage by a director who claimed "There is not a day that goes by that I don't think about" this film. The designer Adrian created over 100 costumes for a scene in which this film abruptly goes silent before the camera pushes through a door to a pond of huge lily pads. A character originally from this film floats above Sailor as he lies in the road in (*) Wild at Heart, one of many allusions to this film by David Lynch. In this film, castle guards with spears chant "O-Ee-Yah! Ee-Oh-Ah!" in the "March of the Winkies." In the so-called "greatest year in film history," both Gone with the Wind and this film were directed by Victor Fleming. For 10 points, a sepia tornado gives way to Technicolor in what 1939 film that features a yellow brick road?
items.a: The Wizard of Oz

items.q: In this film, cinematographer Gregg Toland pioneered a "deep" technique in which all elements are in focus. A flashback in this film shows the protagonist's mother becoming wealthy after one of her tenants gives her a mine in Colorado. This film's protagonist arranges for the building of an opera house for his lover Susan (*) Alexander, whose affair with her ruins his chances to run for governor of New York. This film follows a reporter investigating the meaning of the title character's enigmatic last word, "Rosebud." For 10 points, name this 1941 film directed by Orson Welles about a wealthy newspaper magnate.
items.a: Citizen Kane

items.q: One character in this film meets her future husband while on toothache medication and after splashing mud on him. After being paid for the right to mine gold on her land, one character in this film sends her son away to be raised by the banker Walter Parks Thatcher. The main character of this film builds on opera house for his second wife (*) Susan Alexander and has the circumstances of his death investigated by Jerry Thompson. As he dies at his Xanadu estate, the title character of this film refers to his childhood sled. For 10 points, name this Orson Welles film where the title newspaper mogul's last word is "Rosebud."
items.a: Citizen Kane

items.q: In a flashback experienced by a butler in this movie, the protagonist is shown destroying his 2nd wife's bedroom after she leaves him, while a sequence of breakfast scenes in this film show the deterioration of that man's first marriage to Emily. The death of this film's namesake at (*) Xanadu happens as he drops a snowglobe and says the name of a beloved childhood toy. Reporter Jerry Thompson never discovers that Rosebud is a sled in this movie. For 10 points, name this film starring Orson Welles that was partly inspired by the life of William Randolph Hearst.
items.a: Citizen Kane

items.q: This film's pioneering style of composition and focus was orchestrated by Gregg Toland. The protagonist of this film loses both his marriage and a gubernatorial campaign after his affair with Susan Alexander is revealed, though Alexander eventually leaves him after an unhappy (*) opera career. The Xanadu estate is one setting for this movie, and the biggest mystery in this film is revealed by a sled being thrown into a furnace. For 10 points, name this 1941 movie starring and directed by Orson Welles and whose titular newspaper mogul dies after saying "Rosebud."
items.a: Citizen Kane

items.q: In Twin Peaks: The Return, Agent Cooper sticks a fork in a power outlet after hearing a character in this film say "Get me Gordon Cole." Buster Keaton has a cameo in this film as one of three bridge players. This film's protagonist is mistaken for an undertaker who is hired to bury a chimpanzee. A character in this film responds to the claim "You used to be big" with "I (*) am big. It's the pictures that got small." This film is narrated by the dead protagonist, who is first seen facedown in a swimming pool. This film ends with a character played by Gloria Swanson looking at news cameras and saying "Mr. Demille, I'm ready for my closeup." For 10 points, name this 1950 Billy Wilder film about the aging silent film star Norma Desmond, named for a Los Angeles street.
items.a: Sunset Boulevard

items.q: This movie's opening was originally set in a morgue where a corpse talks to other dead bodies. This movie's narrator has a nightmare about an organ grinder after witnessing the midnight funeral of a pet chimpanzee. Buster Keaton appears in this movie as a member of the "waxworks" who play bridge with its main character, who attempts to seduce the narrator at a New Year's Eve party where he is the only guest. Erich von Stroheim plays the butler Max von Mayerling in this movie, whose narrator is initially hired to work on a version of Salome before becoming the protagonist's kept man. William Holden revived his career by playing this movie's character Joe Gillis, who is seen lying dead in a swimming pool in this movie's opening scene; after his death, the protagonist mistakes news cameras for movie cameras and proclaims "All right, Mr. De Mille, I'm ready for my close-up." For 10 points, name this 1950 Billy Wilder movie about the silent movie star Norma Desmond, which is set on the title street.
items.a: Sunset Boulevard

items.q: Gossip columnist Hedda Hopper makes a cameo appearance in the media circus at the end of this film, and Buster Keaton makes another cameo as one of the "wax works" that plays bridge. After a short car chase, the protagonist is mistaken for the undertaker of a chimpanzee; after confessing that he is only a writer, he is hired to write a film version of Salome. The protagonist of this film is confined to a (*) mansion while working, but manages to escape nightly to meet with Betty Schafer for another script. Beginning with a corpse floating upside down in a swimming pool, this work sees Joe Gillis finishes the script intended for the eccentric Norma Desmond, who uses her connections from the silent era to meet with a director. Starring William Holden as a writer who becomes the love interest of Gloria Swanson, for 10 points, name this Billy Wilder film noir that sees the delivery of the line "Mr. DeMille, I'm ready for my close-up," and at a house on a certain Los Angeles street.
items.a: Sunset Boulevard

items.q: Shortly after this film's protagonist reunites with his wife, the arrival of another character prompts a mute servant to fall on her knees and whisper "It is finished". That protagonist meets a girl who will be burned at the stake shortly after he is tricked into revealing a secret in a confessional booth. In the final scene of this film, a man with an (*) hourglass leads a silhouetted group in a danse macabre. In this film, two married actors seek shelter from the plague with the crusader Antonius Block, who is played by Max von Sydow. For 10 points, name this Ingmar Bergman film about a knight who challenges Death to a game of chess.
items.a: The Seventh Seal [or Det sjunde inseglet ("day HOON-day in-SIG-let")]

items.q: In this film, sunlight shines onto the body of a man the moment he drops dead after writhing on the ground begging for water. In this film, a squirrel hops onto the stump of a tree that had just been cut down, which killed the man hiding in it. After a character in this film gives a painkilling drug to a girl, his friend remarks that the girl's eyes can see nothing but "emptiness under the moon." A character in this film mistakenly reveals his strategy at a (*) confession, and then decides to guide a traveling troupe of actors whose performance had been interrupted by a procession of flagellants. Jof and Mia escape the plague at this film's end and witness a group of dancing figures on a hill. For 10 points, name this Ingmar Bergman film about the knight Antonius Block and his chess match with Death.
items.a: The Seventh Seal [or Det sjunde inseglet]

items.q: In one scene from this film, the main characters share wild strawberries and milk while Jof (Yof) sings about spring. In another scene in this film, Raval steals a bracelet from a dead woman then attempts to rape the servant girl, but is stopped by Jons (Yonz). And in that scene in this film the protagonist claims that "to believe is to suffer". This film closes with its characters performing a danse macabre. In this film, Max von Sydow plays a character who has just returned from the Crusades, named Antonius Block. For 10 points, name this 1957 film by Ingmar Bergman, in which a knight challenges Death to a game of chess.
items.a: The Seventh Seal [or Det Sjunde Inseglet] <JG>

items.q: One character in this movie is a blacksmith whose wife Lisa takes on the name Ariadne while having an extra marital affair. One figure comes in possession of an armlet during a commotion which sees the death of Ravel, while in one scene, the protagonist is offered milk and strawberries after he is introduced to young Michael, the son of Mia and Jof. The protagonist meets a troupe of acrobats traveling for a show at Elsinore, and throughout the movie, the protagonist sees flagellants. For 10 points, name this movie in which Antonius Block is a knight returning from the crusades who plays chess with death, directed by Ingmar Bergman.
items.a: The Seventh Seal [or Det Sjunde Inseglet]

items.q: In one scene from this film, a baker is told to throw away a bouquet of flowers, making it look like he is guarding a hospital entrance. While driving to his sister's apartment ahead of his bodyguards, one character in this film is ambushed at a toll booth. A fish in a bulletproof vest is delivered in this film, signifying the death of (*) Luca Brasi. One character in this film flees to Sicily after shooting Virgil Sollozzo and Captain McCluskey at a restaurant; that character, Michael, succeeds his father, Vito, as don of his family. For 10 points, name this Francis Ford Coppola film, the first in a trilogy depicting the Corleone family.
items.a: The Godfather

items.q: At the last minute, the composer of this film's soundtrack lost his Academy Award nomination after it was learned that he adapted music from the film Fortunella. A wedding in this film features a clip of the aria "Non so piu cosa son" from The Marriage of Figaro and a mazurka dance. A melodic English horn solo opens a "Pastorale" played in this film as a character visits his father in the hospital. This film's title sequence begins with a (*) trumpet playing a slow triple-meter dance composed by Nino Rota, who also published the song "Speak Softly, Now," which is called this film's "Love Theme". It begins with an iconic opening waltz and features the singing of "I Have but One Heart" by Johnny Fontane. For 10 points, name this Francis Ford Coppola film about the Corleone family.
items.a: The Godfather

items.q: In this film, the camera tracks away to an empty hallway while the protagonist apologises on the phone for ruining a date. This film's protagonist jokes about getting "organezized" while on a date with a campaign fundraiser. This was Paul Schrader's first major screenwriting credit, and it starred a 14 year-old Jodie Foster as a prostitute. This film's protagonist improvises a gadget to quickly draw a (*) revolver, which he practices while repeating the line "You talkin' to me?", and he says that "all the animals come out at night" to describe the "scum" of New York city. Robert De Niro starred in-for 10 points-what Martin Scorsese film whose title character tries to shoot one of his passengers?
items.a: Taxi Driver

items.q: Two characters in this film argue over whether "we" or "are" should be underlined in the campaign slogan "We are the people." This film's director makes a cameo appearance as a man spying on his wife, who is cheating on him with a black man. The main character flirts with a girl employed by Senator Palantine but she rejects him after he takes her to see a Swedish (*) sex education film. After shaving his hair into a mohawk, the main character goes on a rampage to rescue Iris, a child prostitute played by Jodie Foster. In its most famous scene, the main character, Travis Bickle, looks at himself in the mirror and asks "You talkin' to me?" For 10 points, name this Martin Scorsese-directed film starring Robert De Niro as a violent cabbie.
items.a: Taxi Driver

items.q: Roberto Benigni plays a member of this profession who gives a priest a heart attack by confessing that he has had sex with a pumpkin, a sheep, and his brother's wife. The director Jafar Panahi plays a member of this profession in the film that won the Golden Bear at the 2015 Berlin Film Festival. Each segment of Jim Jarmusch's Night on Earth focuses on a member of this profession. A member of this profession named (*) Wizard says "You get a job, you become the job" to another member of this profession, who takes a date to see the Swedish sex film Language of Love. A character with this profession attempts to assassinate Senator Palantine and tries to help the teenage prostitute Iris. For 10 points, name this profession of Travis Bickle in a Martin Scorsese film.
items.a: taxi drivers [or:cab drivers, cabbies]

items.q: After the protagonist of this film beats a character who asks to be hit during sex, the camera zooms in on that woman's red lips before cutting to an image of a blazing fire. A David Foster Wallace essay about this film's director argues that Reservoir Dogs references a scene in it in which a gay night club owner lip-syncs Roy Orbison's "In Dreams." This film opens with the camera panning down from a blue sky onto red roses in front of a white picket fence. In this film's final scene, a (*) robin appears holding an insect in its mouth, echoing Sandy's dream in which robins purge the world of insects. This film contains a scene in which a character shouts "Don't you fucking look at me!" while ritualistically raping Dorothy Vallens. The camera slowly zooms in on a severed human ear covered in ants in one scene in this film. For 10 points, Jeffrey Beumont shoots the gas-huffing gangster Frank Booth at the end of what film by David Lynch?
items.a: Blue Velvet

items.q: David Weir argues that this work's image of an Acherontia inspired the depiction of an anopheles mosquito that its creator made four years later for a documentary depicting poor mountain-dwelling peasants called Land Without Bread. A shot of a sea urchin in this movie occurs after a transition from a shot showing the armpit hair of a woman played by Simone Mareuil (mah-RUH-ee). A man drags two grand pianos filled with (*) donkey carcasses in a scene from this movie, which earlier depicts a man poking a severed human hand with his cane. This film's makers later collaborated on the film The Golden Age, and it includes an early scene in which an eye is cut with a razor. For 10 points, name this plotless surrealist film, a collaboration between Luis Bunuel and Salvador Dali.
items.a: Un Chien Andalou [or An Andalusian Dog]

items.q: The son of this film's director claims that Charlie Chaplin's Chinese projectionist would faint every time he showed this movie. A scene set "eight years later" in this film shows a man with a metal box strapped around his neck bicycling down the street dressed in a nun's habit. An androgynous woman pokes at a severed hand with a cane in this film, only to be hit by a car; one of the two figures watching her from an upstairs window then drags two pianos filled with decaying dead donkeys across the room. The most recognizable scene in this film shows a woman's eyeball slowly cut by a razor blade. For 10 points, name this surrealist 1921 film, a collaboration between Salvador Dali and Luis Bunuel.
items.a: Un chien andalou [or An Andalusian Dog]

items.q: At one point in this film, a woman discovers a hand lying in the street and pokes at it with a cane. A notable shot from this film is intercut with images of a cloud passing over the moon and is followed by a meaningless title card reading "eight years later." For 10 points, name this movie; which also contains ants crawling over an injured hand and a man dragging a piano full of dead donkeys across a stage, but is most noted for simulating a razor cutting the eye of a woman; a landmark in Surrealist cinema created by Luis Bunuel and Salvador Dali.
items.a: Un Chien Andalou [or An Andalusian Dog]

items.q: One of its creators claimed that, at its premiere, he filled his pockets with rocks to throw at the audience. The concept arose from a dream in which a cloud slices the moon in half. Eight years after the first scene takes place, a transvestite nun played by one of the creators falls dead while riding a bicycle. A woman defends herself from a sexual assault with a tennis-racket in this film, which also includes scenes of ants crawling from a man's hand and a man pulling a piano loaded down with two priests and a dead donkey. For 10 points, name this film in which a woman randomly has her eye sliced open by a razor, a surrealist work by Luis Bunuel and Salvador Dali.
items.a: "Un Chien Andalou" [or "an Andalusian dog"]

items.q: In one work, this director played a man who witnesses a David Bowie-played character rant about Judy before the scene is merged with visions of the Jumping Man. This director's debut feature opens with a giant sperm leaving the mouth of a Jack Nance-played character. A severed human ear is discovered at the beginning of a film by this director in which a woman dances on a car to (*) "In Dreams" by Roy Orbison while Frank Booth kisses and beats Jeffrey. In a film by this director, a pair of lesbian lovers are told "everything is a recording" in Club Silencio. This director's regular collaborator Kyle MacLachlan starred in a TV show he made in which Detective Dale Cooper investigates Laura Palmer's murder. For 10 points, Blue Velvet and Mulholland Drive are films by which American filmmaker, who co-created Twin Peaks?
items.a: David Lynch <PDC, Other Fine Arts>

items.q: This director filmed a single 13-minute shot of a head of cheese in front of power lines for a film that debuted at the Festival of Disruption. In a twenty-minute long film, this author of the book Catching the Big Fish recalls helping a European girl drink her first Coke and buying colored sugar water in the middle of nowhere in Yugoslavia. This director, who is the better known of the two co-creators of a character who often praises the merits of a "damn fine cup of (*) coffee," was once filmed cooking broccoli and quinoa. Every day at 2:30 pm for seven years, this director ordered a chocolate milkshake at Bob's Big Boy diner. A fast food customer inspired this director to create a character who exclaims "Heineken? Fuck that shit! Pabst! Blue! Ribbon!" For 10 points, a creepy monster emerges from behind a diner in what director's film Mulholland Drive?
items.a: David Lynch [or David Keith Lynch] (The characters mentioned are Dale Cooper from Twin Peaks and Frank Booth from Blue Velvet.)

items.q: In a film by this man, a movie director is interrogated at a corral about the claim that "a man's attitude goes some ways the way his life will be" by "The Cowboy." In a film by this director, after a trumpet player collapses mid-performance, the music continues playing in a scene set at Club Silencio. A character faints after finding a hairy monster behind (*) Winkies diner in a scene from a film by this director, which opens with Rita losing her memories after a car crashes into her limousine on the title road in the Hollywood Hills. For 10 points, what surrealist director of Mulholland Drive also created the TV show Twin Peaks?
items.a: David Lynch

items.q: In one of this director's films, Cherubini's Requiem in C Minor accompanies a murder in a train car, after which the killer gives up his garmonbozia. One of his film's opening sequences ends with an extreme close-up of beetles warring in the grass. In another of his films, the opening of a mysterious blue box causes most characters to shift identities. He created a nightclub singer who is ritualistically raped as Jeffrey Beaumont watches from the closet, and he worked with Mark Frost on a popular television series. For 10 points, name this American director of Mulholland Dr. and Blue Velvet who created Twin Peaks.
items.a: David Lynch

items.q: In a scene from one of this director's films, the repeated sound of firecrackers make three characters on a couch increasingly nervous about the gun wielded by a drug dealer. That film by this director opens with a three minute steadicam shot which moves from a city street to the inside of a disco club. In a different film by this director, the central couple meet after a man orders an incredible amount of (*) breakfast food, causing the waitress to call him a "hungry boy." That waitress turned model later poisons the designer Reynolds Woodcock in this director's most recent film Phantom Thread. For 10 points, name this contemporary American director known for long films like Boogie Nights, Magnolia, and There Will Be Blood.
items.a: Paul Thomas Anderson [prompt on PTA]

items.q: A film by this director pairs shot of a man tossing food in the air to birds circling over a castle with shots of a brass section recording music. On their latest film, Robert Elswit was unavailable so this director shared cinematography responsibilities, including pushing the film stock and adding haze to avoid "looking like The Crown". In a film, this director's camera whip pans away from a close-up of a prostitute talking to the protagonist at a diner to a teenage boy ditching two girls at another table. The last shot of one of this director's films slowly zooms in on Melora Walters sitting in bed before she looks down and then (*) smiles at the camera. This director's 1997 film begins with a long tracking shot that follows characters played by Luis Guzman and Burt Reynolds through a disco club, before ending with an introduction of Reynold's character to the young protagonist played by Mark Wahlberg. That film by this director follows the career of young porn star Dirk Diggler. For 10 points, identify this American director behind the films There Will Be Blood and Boogie Nights.
items.a: Paul Thomas Anderson

items.q: 9. This province was formally claimed by Humphrey Gilbert. The extinct Beothuk ("BEE-uh-thuk") people lived in what is now this province. South of this province are the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon ("MEEK-lohn"). This province's town of Gander was the sight of many redirected (*) flights during 9/11, which is depicted in the musical Come From Away. This province contains L'Anse Aux Meadows ("LANS-oh MEH-dohz"), where the Viking city of Vinland ("VIN-luhnd") was found. For 10 points, name this easternmost Canadian province whose capital is Saint John's.
items.a: Newfoundland and Labrador

items.q: The Long Range Mountains extend along part of this province and include Gros Morne (grow MORN) National Park on the Great Northern Peninsula. The Strait of Belle Isle separates two parts of this province. This province's town of Port-aux-Basque (port oh bosk) was damaged by Hurricane Fiona. (*) Signal Hill overlooks this province's capital, which developed in part due to Grand Banks fisheries. This province's L'Anse Aux Meadows (LAHNS oh MED-oh) was settled by the Vikings. For 10 points, name this island-and-mainland province governed from St. John's.
items.a: Newfoundland and Labrador

items.q: A Commission of Government was formed after this polity's 1934 bankruptcy, and was abolished by Joey Smallwood's Confederate Association in 1949. A company that caused a scandal in the British government had made a technological breakthrough at Signal Hill in this polity. This region was claimed for Britain by Humphrey Gilbert and was once populated by the Beothuk people. One early explorer of this region claimed to be able to catch (*) cod with buckets on the rich Grand Banks fisheries to its southeast; that explorer was John Cabot. This region contains L'Anse aux Meadows, which was probably attacked by Skraelings and formed part of Vinland. For 10 points, name this Atlantic Canadian province whose capital St. John's lies on a namesake island across from Labrador.
items.a: Newfoundland and Labrador [or Terre-Neuve et Labrador; or Dominion of Newfoundland; or Newfoundland Island; or New Found Land; prompt on "Vinland" before it is read; do not accept or prompt on "Labrador"]

items.q: The "Thirty Mile" section of a river with this name extends from Lake Laberge to the Teslin River. A region with this name is crossed by the Pelly and Stewart Rivers and houses the towns of Faro and Carmacks. This name is given to a river that passes by (*) Dawson City and was a route during the Klondike Gold Rush. A territory with this name is governed from Whitehorse and is located directly north of British Columbia. For 10 points, give this shared name of a Canadian river and a territory that borders Alaska to the east.
items.a: Yukon [or Yukon Territory; or Yukon River]

items.q: A poem set in this region declares, "that night on the marge of Lake Lebarge / I cremated Sam McGee," and is by this region's "bard," Robert Service. At the end of a story set in this region, the narrator murmurs "You were right" to the old man of Sulphur Creek. A character who is transported from California's Santa Clara Valley to work in this region watches most of his companions die while working for Hal and Mercedes. A character (*) freezes to death in this region in the story "To Build a Fire." John Thornton frees Buck from working as a sled dog for miners exploring this region. For 10 points, The Call of the Wild is set during a gold rush in what territory in northwest Canada?
items.a: the Yukon [or Yukon Territory; accept the Klondike; accept Yukon Trail or Yukon Gold Rush or Klondike Trail or Klondike River or Klondike Gold Rush; prompt on Canada; prompt on northern Canadaor western Canada or northwest Canada or similar answers by asking, "What specific named region?"; reject "Northwest Territories"]

items.q: Tourist attractions in this region include the Sign Post Forest and the "World's Largest Weathervane," an entire Douglas DC-3 aircraft on a rotating pedestal. Visitors to the Sourdough Saloon can try the Sourtoe Cocktail, seasoned with a preserved amputated human toe, in one town in this region. This region's capital is home to a 58-foot-tall, three-story "log skyscraper" which was built during a housing shortage caused by an influx of workers on a World War II project to build a (*) road to Alaska. Tourists in this territory's Kluane National Park can visit Canada's highest mountain, Mount Logan. This territory's town of Dawson City contains historic buildings built during the Klondike Gold Rush. For 10 points, name this westernmost Canadian territory, whose capital and largest city is Whitehorse.
items.a: Yukon

items.q: The world's largest open-pit zinc and lead mine is located in this region's town of Faro. In this area, a group known as the "Sourdoughs" were based near Lynn Canal. Settlements such as Circle City and (*) Dawson City bloomed in this territory due to the discovery of a certain precious metal. This territory was the site of a namesake gold rush based in the Klondike region. For 10 points, name this Canadian federal territory that borders the US state of Alaska with capital at Whitehorse.
items.a: Yukon

items.q: The finale of Haydn's 98th symphony features a solo for this instrument written for Johann Peter Salomon. A long solo for this instrument represents the Holy Spirit descending to Earth in the Benedictus of Beethoven's Missa solemnis. The Olympic Lodge Orchestra was directed by a player of this instrument, a Guadeloupean fencer titled the Chevalier de Saint-Georges ("sheh-VAL-ee-ay duh SAHN ZHORZH"). Two of these instruments play an F-sharp major duet after the other musicians have left the stage in (*) Haydn's "Farewell" symphony. Joseph Joachim ("YO-seff yo-ah-keem") revived interest in Beethoven's only concerto for this instrument, in D major, which has been recorded by Jascha Heifetz ("YA-sha HIGH-fitz") and Itzhak Perlman. For 10 points, the concertmaster plays what highest-pitched string instrument?
items.a: violin

items.q: In one musical tradition, this instrument is called "behala" and players typically rest its top on their right foot while sitting cross-legged. In a piece written to "nationalize" this instrument, a high D represents one of its title characters jumping into a grave. The sitarist Ravi Shankar and a player of this instrument collaborated on the album (*) West Meets East. A language-based method for learning this instrument was created by a Japanese pedagogue to teach young children. The Chinese erhu often replaces this instrument as the soloist in the Butterfly Lovers' Concerto, written for this instrument. For 10 points, the Suzuki method is a common way to teach what highest-pitched string instrument in the orchestra?
items.a: violins [accept fiddles; prompt on string instruments]

items.q: A virtuosic piece for this instrument and continuo is attributed to Tomaso Antonio Vitali, though its wild key shifts suggest it may be a musical hoax. Eugene Ysaye's ("ee-ZAH-eez") second sonata for this instrument begins with a quote from Bach's third E-major partita for this instrument. A set of sonnets accompanied the publication of a set of (*) concerti for this instrument, the score for which included captions comparing certain passages to "drunkards asleep" and a "barking dog." Antonio Vivaldi wrote over 200 concertos for this instrument, including ones titled "Spring" and "Summer." For 10 points, The Four Seasons are a set of concerti for what string instrument?
items.a: violin

items.q: A Romani-inspired melody opens the first of Three Romances dedicated to a player of this instrument by Clara Schumann. This instrument and the accompaniment open the finale of one sonata by playing the quarter notes [read slowly] "B, C-sharp," then "A, G-sharp, F-sharp, long E" in canon. A player of this instrument wrote a set of six sonatas each incorporating the style of players like Joseph Szigeti and George Enescu. The motto "free but lonely" lends the nickname F-A-E to a sonata for this instrument collaboratively written by Johannes Brahms and Robert Schumann. Cesar Franck ("fronk") wrote an A major sonata for this instrument as a wedding gift for Eugene Ysaye ("oo-ZHEN ee-ZYE"), a virtuoso of this instrument. A Beethoven sonata for this instrument is dedicated to Rodolphe Kreutzer. For 10 points, Joseph Joachim ("YO-sef YO-ah-kim") played what highest-pitched string instrument?
items.a: violin

items.q: A concerto for this non-clarinet instrument was called a composer's "Eroica" by Alfred Einstein, who claimed Johann Andre finished another concerto for it. A composer who wrote a "Sonata facile" ("fah-CHEE-lay") for this instrument included a theme opening "B, A, G-sharp, A, C" to imitate Janissary bands in the last movement of another sonata. This is the original instrument for which Mozart's variations on the tune of (*) "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" were written. The "Rondo alla turca" appears in the last movement of the 11th sonata for this instrument by Mozart, who also composed 27 concertos for it. For 10 points, name this keyboard instrument with 88 black and white keys.
items.a: piano [or pianoforte]

items.q: Alicia de Larrocha made the first complete recording of a piece for this instrument that contrasts A-flat minor and A-flat major in its opening Evocacion ("eh-vo-ca-see-OWN"). The song "Besame Mucho" was inspired by "The Maiden and the Nightingale," a piece for this instrument from Enrique Granados' Goyescas. Ricardo Vines premiered a piece for this instrument whose first movement depicts the Generalife ("he-ne-ra-LEE-feh"), Manuel de Falla's ("FA-ya's") (*) Nights in the Gardens of Spain. Basque folk music inspired a G major concerto for this instrument by Maurice Ravel that begins with a whip crack. Paul Wittgenstein premiered Ravel's concerto for the left hand on this instrument. For 10 points, the right pedal is used for sustain on what keyboard instrument?
items.a: piano [or pianoforte] (The piece in the first clue is Isaac Albeniz's Iberia.)

items.q: "Idea 22" was recorded for this instrument by Mexican composer Gibran Alcocer. "Experience" and "Nuvole Bianche" were composed by a player of this instrument named Ludovico Einaudi. Victors of high-profile competitions between players of this instrument include the Texan Van Cliburn and Argentina's Martha Argerich. Nikolai Rubinstein initially detested Tchaikovsky's enduring (*) first concerto for this instrument. A Polish composer who played this instrument was inspired by a dog chasing its own tail to write the "Minute Waltz" for it. Frederic Chopin played, for 10 points, what musical instrument consisting of black and white keys?
items.a: piano [accept piano forte or fortepiano]

items.q: For this instrument, Claude Debussy ["DEH-boo-see"] wrote the prelude "The Girl With The Flaxen Hair" and the suite Children's Corner. Erik Satie's ambient pieces for this instrument include three Gnossiennes["NOH-si-ENS"] and Gymnopedie No. 1 ["JEEM-noh-ped-ee number one"]. The third movement of Suite bergamasque ["BEHR-ga-mask"], a suite for this instrument, heavily uses this instrument's (*) right-foot sustain pedal and has a French name meaning "moonlight." Debussy's "Clair de lune" is for this instrument. For 10 points, name this keyboard instrument with 88 keys.
items.a: piano [or pianoforte]

items.q: Twelve sonatas by Domenico Scarlatti were adapted into works in this genre by the author of the first work on musical criticism published in English, Charles Avison, who was influenced by his teacher Francesco Geminiani. The final movement of a piece in this genre intersperses a minuet with two trios and a polacca, or a polonaise. The second movement of another piece in this genre consists of a single (*) measure with two chords that make up a Phrygian half cadence. Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni commissioned a piece in this genre that ends with a G-major 12/8 ("twelve-eight") time pastorale ad libitum movement. Arcangelo Corelli composed that G-minor piece in this genre "for the night of Christmas." J. S. Bach wrote six pieces dedicated to the margrave of Brandenburg in, for 10 points, what genre?
items.a: concerto [or concerto grosso; accept Christmas Concerto; accept Brandenburg Concertos; do not accept or prompt on concertos for any solo instruments]

items.q: Edward Elgar's only work for cello in this musical genre was popularized by Jacqueline du Pr´e. A set of these works for keyboard is dedicated to Christian Ludwig. Vivaldi wrote a set of pieces in this genre, The Contest Between Harmony and Invention, that includes (*) four of them collectively called The Four Seasons, and features violin. For 10 points, name this genre of music in which a solo instrument is featured with a backing orchestra, exemplified by Bach's Brandenburg ones.
items.a: concertos (accept concerti; accept cello concerto; accept piano concerto; accept Emperor Concerto; accept violin concerto)

items.q: One piece in this genre famously begins with the timpani quietly playing five Ds. A formally innovative early Mozart piece in this genre was nicknamed "Jeunehomme." Mozart wrote four of these pieces for Joseph Leutgeb. Another Mozart piece in this genre became known for its appearance in the movie Elvira Madigan ; he also played one of these pieces at Leopold II's (*) coronation. Beethoven's last work for piano in this genre has been nicknamed "Emperor." Mozart's last work in this genre was written for clarinettist Anton Stadler. For 10 points, name this orchestral genre that usually features a virtuoso soloist.
items.a: concertos [or concerti; accept violin concerto; accept piano concertos; accept clarinet concertos; accept horn concertos]

items.q: One of these musical works features a harpsichord cadenza that was probably played by J.S. Bach at its premiere. Bela Bartok wrote one of these works for Orchestra. Vivaldi's hundreds of these works include The Four Seasons, and Mozart wrote a (*) double one for flute and harp. For 10 points, name this type of musical work in which a solo instrument is accompanied by an orchestra or other group of supporting instruments.
items.a: concerto [accept Brandenburg Concerto (s) before "Bela Bartok" is mentioned]

items.q: One piece of this type uses the soggetto cavato technique to map an Italian phrase meaning "let me do it" to the solfege ("SOUL-fezh") syllables "La sol fa re mi." A 1917 Hans Pfitzner opera dramatizes the events surrounding a type of these works "without a name." The oldest complete one of these pieces by a single composer was written by Guillaume de Machaut ("ghee-OHM de muh-SHOW"). The cantus firmus "L'homme arme" ("LOHM ar-MAY") was used in two works of this type by (*) Josquin des Prez ("joe-SCAN deh PRAY"). According to legend, a ban on polyphony ("puh-LIF-uh-nee") was avoided after Palestrina wrote a piece of this type named for Pope Marcellus II that contains a two-movement Agnus Dei and opens with a Kyrie ("KEE-ree-ay"). For 10 points, name these choral settings of the liturgy of the Eucharist.
items.a: mass [or missa; accept missa sine nomine; reject "requiem mass"] (The Italian phrase is "Lascia fare mi." The Pfitzner opera is Palestrina.)

items.q: The Flemish composer Guillaume du Fay ("GEE-om doo fai") wrote one of these compositions based on a previous work entitled "If my face is pale". Compositions of this kind that use no previous source material are called '[these works] without a name'. A composition of this type named for Pope Marcellus was apocryphally used to prevent (*) polyphony from being banned at the Council of Trent. Palestrina wrote over 100 of these pieces, which were usually based on a melody called a cantus firmus, and J. S. Bach wrote a famous one of these pieces in B minor. A requiem is one of these works "for the dead." For 10 points, name these sacred compositions that set the liturgy of the Eucharist to music.
items.a: mass [or missa; accept 'missa sine nomine'; or 'masses without a name'; accept Pope Marcellus Mass; accept Cantus Firmus Mass; accept Mass in B Minor]

items.q: The French song "L'homme arme" ("lum ar-MAY") has been used as a cantus firmus for many pieces of this type, including ones by Guillaume Dufay ("ghee-YOWM doo-FAY") and Josquin des Prez ("joe-CAWN day-PRAY"). A "brief" one of these works composed in 1733 for the Elector of Saxony was later reused by its composer for one with a (*) "Dona nobis pacem" movement. Legendarily, a ban on polyphonic music was prevented after Palestrina composed one of these works for Pope Marcellus II. J. S. Bach's only complete work of this type is in B minor. Sections of these works include "Kyrie" ("KEE-ree-ay"), "Gloria," and "Agnus Dei." For 10 points, a requiem is an example of what type of work, which sets to music the liturgy of the Eucharist?
items.a: Mass [or missa; do NOT accept or prompt on "requiem"]

items.q: Uwe Wolf used micro-X-ray fluorescence analysis on a piece in this genre to distinguish its composer's handwriting from later edits as part of a "New Edition" of his work. The second section of that piece of this type begins with the vivace trumpet melody "D, A, D, E, F-sharp-E-D-E." The first four bars of a piece in this genre may be some of the few that do not parody earlier compositions, contrasting it with "sine nomine" pieces that are based entirely on original material. A 27-movement Baroque-era piece in this genre has a roughly symmetrical structure around a central "Crucifixus" movement. Pieces in this choral genre are often divided into the short "brevis" and longer "solemnis" types. For 10 points, name this genre of a B minor piece by J.S. Bach, which sets Catholic liturgy to music.
items.a: mass [or missa or Messe; accept Mass in B minor or Messe in H moll, accept missa sine nomine]

items.q: A G minor piece of this type includes a dotted oboe passage in its second movement representing an animal's jerky head movements, and is part of a set of six premiered by conductor Chevalier de Saint-Georges ("san-ZHORZH"). The final movement of one piece of this type features a five-part fugato centered around the notes [read slowly] C, D, F, E. An F sharp minor piece of this type ends with musicians blowing out their candles and leaving the stage. Joseph Haydn ("HIGH-dun") included a sudden G major chord in the second movement of his 94th piece of this type, allegedly to wake up any sleeping audience members. For 10 points, name these orchestral pieces that include Jupiter by Mozart and Farewell and Surprise by Haydn.
items.a: symphony [or symphonies; accept Jupiter Symphony; accept Farewell Symphony; accept Surprise Symphony]

items.q: Some of the earliest pieces in this genre were written by the Milanese composer Antonio Brioschi [bree-OS-key], who wrote 26 of them. Seventy-eight of these pieces were written by Giovanni Battista Sammartini, who helped shift this genre away from an earlier "Italian" style. With an ensemble partly named the Olympic Lodge, Chevalier de Saint-Georges [che-val-YAY de sahnt george] premiered a set of six of these pieces in Paris. These pieces originally were (*) three movements and were used as overtures in opera houses prior to the developments of Mannheim School composer Johann Stamitz. Classical-era composers began writing pieces in this genre with an opening sonata, a slow movement, a minuet or scherzo, and an allegro or rondo finale. For 10 points, name this long genre for full orchestra, such as Haydn's "Farewell."
items.a: symphony

items.q: A piece of this type by Hector Berlioz uses a repeated "idee fixe" ["ee-DEY feeks"] melody to represent the artist's beloved and includes a "Dream of a Witches' Sabbath." Dmitri Shostakovich wrote his seventh of these pieces in response to the German invasion of Leningrad. Antonin Dvorak's ["duh-VORE-zhak's"] travels in America inspired his ninth of these pieces, "From The New (*) World." It's not string quartets, but Franz Joseph Haydn is called the "Father" of these pieces, because he codified their four-movement structure. For 10 points, name these large-scale orchestral pieces.
items.a: symphony [accept Symphonie fantastique, "Leningrad" Symphony, "New World" Symphony, or Symphony "From the New World"]

items.q: A banjo is included in a piece in this form that quotes Dunbar poems. A "juba dance" was included in pieces of this type by Florence Price. William Grant Still wrote an "Afro-American" one of these pieces. The Song of Hiawatha partially inspired an e minor piece in this form with an allegro con fuoco finale. Harry Burleigh inspired a movement in that piece of this type with an English horn solo which inspired the song (*) "Goin' home." Like the American String Quartet, that piece of this type was influenced by its composer's stay in Iowa. For 10 points, African-American music inspired Antonin Dvorak's 9th piece in what form, known as "New World."
items.a: symphony [or symphonies; accept Tales: A Folklore Symphony; accept Afro-American Symphony or William Grant Still's Symphony No. 1 in A-flat major; accept Florence Price's Symphony No. 1 in e minor; accept the New World Symphony or Antonin Dvorak's Symphony No. 9 in e minor] (the second line refers to the Afro-American Symphony)

items.q: It's not a prelude or fugue, but Johann Christian Schickhardt composed a collection of these works in all 24 keys. It's not a suite, but baroque "da camera" versions of these works consisted of several short dances and were contrasted with their "da chiesa" type, a distinction largely cemented by the work of Arcangelo Corelli. (*) 555 works of this type for solo harpsichord were published by Domenico Scarlatti. By the classical period, pieces of this type began to include a well-defined exposition, development, and recapitulation. For 10 points, pieces of what form for the piano include one by Beethoven nicknamed "Moonlight"?
items.a: sonatas

items.q: Heinrich Biber included a notable passacaglia for solo violin in his Rosary pieces of this genre. Corelli's first four opuses showcase these works "da camera" and "da chiesa"; those compositions are trio variants of these pieces. Another of these pieces with a lyrical A-flat major Adagio cantabile begins with a Grave [grav-ay] C minor chord. Many of these pieces for piano were also written by Muzio (*) Clementi. Although only a few were in these pieces' Classical "Allegro" form with an exposition, development, and recapitulation, Domenico Scarlatti wrote 555 of these pieces. For 10 points, name this musical genre, examples of which include Beethoven's Pathetique and Moonlight.
items.a: sonata [accept piano sonata]

items.q: The last of an Opus 5 collection of twelve pieces in this genre consists of 23 variations on "La Folia"; that set of works of this type was written by Arcangelo Corelli. Two violins play over continuo in Corelli's "trio" pieces in this genre. After giving his bow and instrument to Satan in a dream, Giuseppe Tartini wrote a work in this genre now nicknamed "Devil's Trill." 555 keyboard pieces of this type were written by Domenico Scarlatti. Later examples of this broad genre that use piano in place of continuo include Beethoven's Kreutzer ("KROY-tser"). For 10 points, identify this genre of instrumental music for a solo instrument without orchestral backing, contrasted with the sung cantata.
items.a: sonatas [accept violin sonata, trio sonata, keyboard sonata, or keyboard sonata; accept harpsichord sonata]

items.q: One work of this type takes its name come from the German word for piano and starts with a series of chords in B Flat Major and later in D Major. Another work of this type was known as "Appassionata." Lebewohl were the words to the first three chords in one type of this work that was written for the fleeing of Archduke (*) Randolph. Along with "Les Adieux," one work of this type features an adagio sostenuto first movement where the right hand plays triplets and was nicknamed "Quasi una Fantasia." For 10 points, name this type of work which includes a "Moonlight" variety written by Beethoven.
items.a: Sonata

items.q: This sculptor created a mattress for a Roman sculpture discovered at the Santa Maria della Vittoria. An unfinished sculpture by this artist depicts a woman holding the Sun while standing on the Earth. Sculptures of the Cornaro family occupy a balcony and watch over this artist's depiction of a "dart of love." This artist's several works for the Borghese Gallery include one of Pluto carrying away Prosperina and another of Daphne turning into a tree. This sculptor of Truth Unveiled by Time depicted golden rays falling on an angel as he prepares to thrust his spear into a nun. For 10 points, name this Italian Baroque sculptor of The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa.
items.a: Gian Lorenzo Bernini

items.q: John Evlyn's diaries described how this artist designed special effects in which a theater caught fire, but transformed into a garden. This artist was inspired by Stromboli's eruption to design the first annual fireworks display at the Castel Sant'Angelo. In a tomb designed by this artist, a billowing jasper cloak traps a skeleton who holds an hourglass. This artist placed putti above a lay woman who reclines on a pillow and grasps her heart in a sculpture for the (*) Altieri Chapel depicting Ludovica Albertoni. At age 81, this artist finished the tomb of Alexander VII. Portraits of donors in theater boxes flank a sculpture by this artist in the Cornaro Chapel which shows an angel standing over a woman on a cloud. For 10 points, name this sculptor who depicted an arrow pointed at a nun in The Ecstasy of St. Theresa.
items.a: Gian Lorenzo Bernini

items.q: The Trastevere district of one city contains this man's depiction of a local mystic, Blessed Ludovica Albertoni . A bronze dove tops a sculpture by this artist which centers on an Egyptian obelisk. A two-figure work by this artist is located in the Santa Maria della Vittoria's Cornaro Chapel, while Rome's (*) Piazza Navona is home to his allegory of the Danube, Nile, Ganges, and Rio de la Plata. This sculptor of the Fountain ofthe Four Rivers is best known for a depiction of a Spanish saint being euphorically pierced by an angel's spear. For 10 points, name this Italian sculptor of The Ecstasy of St. Theresa.
items.a: Gian Lorenzo Bernini

items.q: One of this artist's unfinished works depicts a nude woman holding a face representing the sun, and was originally supposed to depict Time disrobing her. Death raises an hourglass in a tomb by this artist, which shows Truth putting their foot on England on a globe to represent Alexander VII ("the seventh") subduing Anglicanism. An Egyptian obelisk with the Pamphili (pam-FEE-lee) family emblem appears behind gods representing the (*) Rio de la Plata, Nile, Danube, and Ganges in this artist's Fountain of the Four Rivers. Another of their works stands in the Santa Maria della Vittoria's Cornaro Chapel and depicts an angel pointing an arrow at a swooning nun. For 10 points, name this Baroque sculptor of The Ecstasy of St. Theresa.
items.a: Gian Lorenzo Bernini

items.q: A black and a red shape clash in one of this artist's late abstract paintings, which makes up a series with Gay Forms, Playing Forms, and Broken Forms. This artist of Fighting Forms painted birds sitting on a tree branch beneath a waterfall in a painting inspired by his visit to the Italian town of Merano, The Bewitched Mill. On a postcard of one of his paintings, this artist called it a "premonition" that "I can hardly conceive that I painted"; that painting has the words "And all being is flaming suffering" written on its back. A painting by this artist that disappeared after being obtained by Hermann Goering depicts a rainbow above a (*) "tower" of certain creatures. Three years before his death in World War I, he created a chaotic depiction of wolves, foxes, and deer in a forest fire. For 10 points, name this artist of The Fate of the Animals and several paintings of blue horses, a cofounder of Der Blaue Reiter.
items.a: Franz Marc

items.q: One of his paintings shows two red cows, a blue deer, and two green horses. In addition to The Fate of the Animals, this man painted the geometric scene as Stables. Late in life, he painted semi-abstract works such as Tyrol. His admiration for Van Gogh can be seen in his Cats on a Red Cloth, but he may be better known for an association with someone he met in the New Artists Association. For 10 points, name this man who organized the first exhibition of The Blue Rider, including the works of his colleague Wassily Kandinsky.
items.a: Franz Marc

items.q: His collaboration with the poets Carmen Sylva and Richard Dehmel, among others, was published posthumously as Stella Peregrina. While his early work inspired by Van Gogh resulted in such nature studies as Larch Sapling, his later works, including Playing Forms and Fighting Forms, are non-representational. He contributed the essay "Wild Germany" to an artistic almanac released in 1912, and his large compositions include the canvases Mandrill and Fate of Animals. These paintings marked the zenith of his mature approach which depicted prismatically shattered animal forms. For 10 points, identify this artist, whose painting of two equines named the movement he founded with Wasily Kandinsky, The Blue Rider.
items.a: Franz Marc

items.q: After the success of Alexandre Cabanel's Birth of Venus, this painter responded with a set of two paintings, the first of which depicts a masculine Venus lying on top of a sleeping Psyche. In another painting by this artist, a woman holds out her outstretched arm as she receives a parrot. A parody by Tanja Ostojic ("Tanya OSS-toh-yeech") titled "After [this artist]" depicts a set of panties that includes the European Union flag. Two nude lesbians embrace on silk sheets in a painting by this artist entitled Sleep. Jacques Lacan owned, and Khalil Bey commissioned, a painting by this artist that likely features Joanna Hiffernan's exposed vulva. A crucifix is held high above clergymen in a painting by this artist that depicts his uncle's funeral. For 10 points, name this French realist painter of The Origin of the World and The Burial at Ornans.
items.a: Gustave Courbet

items.q: This artist carries a large walking stick in a painting where he meets his patron Alfred Bruyas. This artist runs his hands through his hair in a "desperate" self-portrait. Joanna Hiffernan likely modeled for a painting by this artist that focuses on a woman's genitalia. A painting by this artist shows a man (*) kneeling in front of a priest in black robes and a crucifix being held above the crowd at the title event. In a painting by this artist, two peasant laborers wearing worn-out clothing face away from the viewer and perform the title action. For 10 points, name this Realist artist of A Burial at Ornans and The Stone Breakers .
items.a: Gustave Courbet

items.q: Early depictions of this man can be found in the paintings Man with Leather Belt and The Cellist. This man's appearance references the Wandering Jew in a painting in which he meets a patron and the servant Calas. This man is depicted wildly grasping his hair in The Desperate Man and can be seen painting the Loue River valley at the center of a larger painting. Figures like Alfred Bruyas and Charles (*) Baudelaire surround this painter in that painting subtitled an "allegory summing up 7 years of [his] artistic and moral life." For 10 points, name this French painter who depicted himself in The Artist's Studio, the Realist painter of A Burial at Ornans.
items.a: Gustave Courbet

items.q: A painting by this artist set in his hometown depicts a man in black playing the violin to the right, set After Dinner. This artist painted his sisters Zoe, Zelie, and Juliette assisting a barefoot peasant girl in Young Ladies of the Village. In a painting set in this artist's hometown, two old veterans of the Revolution of '93 stand next to a white dog. A white cat naps beneath a landscape painting being (*) painted by this artist in the center of one painting. This artist included his patron Alfred Bruyas among many Parisian elites next to a nude model watching this artist work in his studio. On the left of one painting by this artist, a crucifix is held high above clergymen next to a man kneeling toward a hole. For 10 points, name this French Realist painter, whose many depictions of his hometown include A Burial at Ornans.
items.a: Gustave Courbet

items.q: Dr. Richard Taylor claims to have detected fractals in this man's paintings through computer-assisted analysis. This student of Thomas Hart Benton gained recognition for his signature painting technique after being photographed in his studio by Hans Namuth. This artist of Autumn Rhythm and (*) Blue Poles was nicknamed "the Dripper" for his technique of action painting. For ten points, name this American abstract expressionist painter of Lavender Mist .
items.a: Jackson Pollock

items.q: Carl Jung's theories may have inspired this artist's early works, like the Native-American-influenced painting The Moon-Woman Cuts the Circle. The myth of Romulus and Remus inspired this artist's painting The She-Wolf, which was painted in an East Hampton studio. Clement Greenberg was introduced to this artist by their wife, Lee Krasner, who had her handprints depicted in the top right of this artist's painting (*) Lavender Mist. This artist's painting Blue Poles was later renamed as Number 11, 1952. For 10 points, name this abstract-expressionist painter known for using his distinctive "drip technique."
items.a: Jackson Pollock [or Paul Jackson Pollock]

items.q: This artist was inspired by Jung's (yoongz) ideas of the anima and animus and a Navajo art exhibit at the MoMA to paint Guardians of the Secret. This artist painted Mural for the entrance to Peggy Guggenheim's townhouse. This artist was often photographed by Hans Namuth while in their studio. This artist's relationship with Ruth Kligman partly led to their divorce from Lee Krasner. Another of their paintings shows eight (*) blue poles and is titled Number 8, 1952. Cigarettes and nails are embedded in another of this artist's paintings titled Full Fathom Five. Autumn Rhythm and Lavender Mist are paintings by this artist. For 10 points, what abstract expressionist is sometimes called "Jack the Dripper"?
items.a: Jackson Pollock [or Paul Jackson Pollock; prompt on Jack "the Dripper" before it is read]

items.q: Marcel Duchamp suggested that this artist paint a large mural scene simply known as Mural on canvas instead of the walls of a New York City townhouse. That work commissioned by Peggy Guggenheim led art critic Clement Greenberg to champion this artist. Hans Namuth took many photos of this artist, who included two handprints in the top right corner of a work that this artist's wife Lee Krasner helped influence. That painting, like many others by this artist, is named for a number and year and is subtitled Lavender Mist. For 10 points, name this Abstract Expressionist whose style of "action painting" resulted from his technique of dripping paint onto canvases.
items.a: Jackson Pollock [or Paul Jackson Pollock; prompt on Jack the Dripper]

items.q: This artist added lines from James Thomson's The Seasons to a painting that caused controversy after being swapped with the painting Caligula's Palace and Bridge. This artist created a smaller, sunnier replica of one painting later gifted to his patron John Fisher. Another painting by this artist created three years after the death of his wife depicts a rainbow amidst a stormy sky above the title building. This artist, who depicted Salisbury Cathedral "from the Meadows" and "from the Bishop's Grounds," created a set of paintings known as "six-footers," including one titled The White Horse. Willy Lott's Cottage appears on the left-hand side of a painting by this artist depicting three horses pulling a wagon of wood across the River Stour. For 10 points, name this Romantic painter of The Hay Wain.
items.a: John Constable

items.q: This artist was known as the "handsome miller" during his time working a windmill, according to his friend C. R. Leslie's biography. This artist exclaimed, "He has been here and fired a gun," when a rival upstaged him on varnishing day with the impromptu addition of a dash of red. The central feature of one of this artist's paintings was covered by a highway in a 2022 reimagining by Just Stop Oil. This amateur meteorologist painted quick sketchings of the sky in his (*) "skying" sessions. The first of this artist's "six footers" shows the title white horse in a boat. This artist's The Leaping Horse depicts the River Stour ("stoor"), which he showed in another painting that features Willy Lott's cottage behind three horses pulling the title agricultural vehicle. For 10 points, name this British artist of The Hay Wain.
items.a: John Constable

items.q: This artist's first successful work was a painting of a horse being ferried across a river. That painting, The White Horse, was the first of this artist's series of "six-footers." One of this painter's works was originally titled Landscape: Noon and depicts his neighbor's cottage on the River (*) Stour [stoor]. This artist painted a double rainbow over Stonehenge in one work and painted multiple renditions of Salisbury Cathedral. Name this British landscape artist who painted The Hay Wain.
items.a: John Constable

items.q: This artist's weather studies include the vaguely Impressionist Seascape Study with Rain Cloud. This artist represented grief over his wife's death in a violent sky in a painting in which a rainbow arcs over a cathedral. The White Horse was the first of this artist's "six-footers," a series depicting the River Stour. He depicted that same river winding in paintings of his hometown of (*) Dedham Vale. This artist painted a common subject of his "from the Meadows" and "from the Bishop's Grounds." Three horses pull the title vehicle in a painting by this artist. For ten points, name this Romantic landscape artist of The Hay Wain.
items.a: John Constable

items.q: Sam Moyers' sculptures Doors for Doris are located near this place. The sculpture Angel of the Waters stands atop a fountain in this location. 7,503 nylon gates were installed in this location by Christo. Frederick Roth's statue of (*) Balto is located here, and Belvedere Castle is located north of the Strawberry Fields and Sheep Meadow in this location. One of the obelisks known as Cleopatra's needle is located in this location, which was designed by Calvert Vaux and Frederick Law Olmsted. For 10 points, name this large park located in Manhattan.
items.a: Central Park [Prompt on New York City]

items.q: In 2017, Ai Weiwei protested U.S border control by placing a giant Gilded Cage in this place. A memorial in this location was designed by Bruce Kelly, who fought to preserve this place. A controversial photo taken here depicts an exasperated child holding a toy hand grenade, and was shot by Diane Arbus. Bright orange structures were installed throughout this location for Jean-Claude and Christo's 2005 installation The Gates. This place, home to one of three of Cleopatra's Needles, was designed by landscape architects Calvert Vaux and Frederick Law Olmsted. For 10 points, name this public space bordering the Met and Guggenheim, a large park in New York City.
items.a: Central Park [prompt on New York City; prompt on NYC; prompt on Manhattan]

items.q: This location is the setting of a Diane Arbus photograph in which a boy holds a toy hand grenade. The sounds of nature which men would hear sitting on a bench in this location "In the Dark" was depicted in a Charles Ives composition titled for this place. This location was the site of an art installation by Christo and Jeanne-Claude that featured over seventy-five hundred gates. This location, which was designed by Calvert Vaux [VAWKS] and Frederick Law Olmsted, is home to an obelisk known as Cleopatra's Needle. For 10 points, name this large park in Manhattan.
items.a: Central Park [prompt on less specific answers such as "Manhattan" or "NYC"]

items.q: Frank Baines reinforced this location's roof after a death-watch beetle infestation damaged the work of Hugh Herland and Henry Yevele ("YEE-vell") in a room filled with a "white hart" emblem. A three-stage staircase based on Bernini's Scala Regia was designed for this location by John Soane after the death of James Wyatt. Part of this location with a historic "hammer-beam roof" was turned from a room to a corridor during renovations which also included the addition of frescoes by William Dyce.
